item.title: Apprenticeship in Lucerne: a practical guide
item.description: Search for internship, salary, social contributions and professional maturity: here's how to orient yourself in Swiss dual training in Lucerne.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Dual apprenticeship: 3-4 years between company and vocational school - Maximum hours 45-50 hours/week, 4-5 weeks of guaranteed vacation - Increasing salary and social contributions from the first day
## Key facts - **What**: Professional training (AFC) in a dual system - Where: Canton of Lucerne, companies and vocational schools - Who: Young people from 15 years old with compulsory education completed - Duration: 3-4 years depending on the profession - Start: Search 1-2 years before the start date - Protection: Federal labor law applies to all apprentices
Apprenticeship in Switzerland is the most widespread professional training path after compulsory schooling. In the Canton of Lucerne, the system operates on a dual basis: the young apprentice spends 60-70% of the time in the company (practical training with a qualified trainer) and 30-40% in a vocational school (theoretical lessons and general culture). This model combines practical skills and knowledge, ensuring that the labor market has figures ready for employment.
The search for the internship usually begins during the penultimate or last year of middle school. The main channels are the official job search sites, direct contact with companies in the sector of interest, training fairs organized by the canton, and school guidance offices. In the Canton of Lucerne, the cantonal vocational training office provides support to both young people and host companies in the matching process between demand and supply.
### The internship contract: rights and duties
The internship contract is the fundamental legal instrument that regulates the relationship between the apprentice, the trainer, and the company. It must be drawn up in writing and contains essential information: total duration, start date, gross monthly salary, weekly working hours, vocational school days, insurances, rights, and duties of both parties.
The trainer commits to providing professional training according to the cantonal training objectives, to carrying out periodic checks of progress, to paying the agreed salary, and to issuing the internship certificate at the end. The apprentice commits to regularly attending lessons and practical training in the company, to respecting the company regulations, to performing the assigned tasks diligently, and to participating in the final exams.
### Legal protection and rights of the apprentice
During the internship, the apprentice enjoys federal legal protection. The maximum working hours are 45 hours per week in the industry, offices, and commerce sectors (50 hours in other sectors). Minimum vacations are guaranteed: 4 weeks per year for apprentices over 20 years old, 5 weeks for under 20 (some cantons and collective sectors provide 5 uniform weeks). Breaks and weekly rest are mandatory according to the federal labor law.
In case of termination, the notice period is 1 month during the first year; from the second year onwards, it increases to 2 months. In cases of serious non-compliance (e.g., systematic violation of training duties), immediate termination with documented justification is possible. During the internship period, the apprentice accumulates mandatory contributions to the federal social security systems (AVS/AHV, unemployment insurance), ensuring protection in case of future illness, injury, or unemployment. ### Compensation and Salary Dynamics
The apprentice's compensation is not set at the federal level: each canton, sector, and company determines the monthly amount independently. In the Canton of Lucerne, as in other Swiss cantons, the salary range for apprentices varies depending on the profession and the chosen VET pathway. Generally, compensation increases year by year: the first year is lower, the second and third years increase progressively, reaching amounts closer to the salary of a qualified professional in the fourth year. Some sectors (e.g., crafts, manufacturing industry, retail trade) have collective wages agreed upon between employers' associations and unions, which establish uniform minimums for the category.
During the apprenticeship, compensation is subject to federal, cantonal, and municipal taxation, according to the Swiss three-tier system. Each canton has its own tax rates, and each municipality acts as a multiplier on the cantonal level. An apprentice residing in the Canton of Lucerne pays federal direct tax based on income (with deductible allowances for young people and students), then Lucerne cantonal tax, and finally a municipal tax on top of the cantonal base.
### Mandatory Social Contributions
From the first month of the apprenticeship, the apprentice is enrolled in the Swiss social security systems. The gross monthly amount received is subject to precise deductions:
- **AVS/AHV and disability insurance (AI)**: 5.3% borne by the employee (apprentice); the employer pays the complementary 5.3%, for a total of 10.6%. These contributions guarantee the right to old-age pension, disability pension, and survivor's benefits. - Unemployment insurance (AD) and insolvency insurance (AC): 1.1% borne by the employee up to an annual maximum (the exact amount varies each year, consult the cantonal office for 2026). Covers protection in case of involuntary job loss. - Accident insurance (LAINF/LAA): 0.7–1.5% borne by the employer, depending on the sector. The apprentice does not pay direct contributions but is automatically covered for work-related accidents and occupational diseases. - Professional pension fund (LPP/BVG): If the company has a pension fund, the apprentice might not be enrolled during the first year (depends on company and cantonal instructions). Some cantons require enrollment from the second year or with a minimum salary threshold.
💡 The sum of these contributions amounts to about 12-15% of the gross salary. The exact percentages for AVS/AI and AD/AC are fixed according to federal laws, while LAINF and LPP vary depending on the sector and company. Consult the Lucerne cantonal office for specific details and applicable amounts for 2026.
### Income Tax and Deductions
The federal direct tax on employment income is progressive and depends on the tax rate of the civil status and asset situation. For an apprentice, usual deductions include: deduction for dependent employment income (amount not specified for 2026, consult AFC/ESTV), travel and accommodation expenses (if necessary to reach the workplace and school), and health insurance premiums (LAMal/KVG). Health insurance must be taken out within 3 months of the start of the apprenticeship (if not already in possession). LAMal premiums depend on the canton, geographical region, age, and chosen deductible (for adults: CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 or 2500). In the Canton of Lucerne, the canton provides [subsidies (cantonal contributions) for premiums](nav:health) for young people and low-income individuals, reducing the economic burden.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Professional Maturity: The Upgrade After AFC
Upon completion of the AFC apprenticeship (3-4 years), the apprentice receives the professional apprentice certificate (Lehrbrief), a nationally recognized document that allows them to practice their profession with verified qualifications. Many apprentices choose to complete a professional maturity program, which can be obtained in parallel during the internship (integrated part-time model) or after the AFC certificate (post-diploma professional maturity). Professional maturity adds theoretical skills and opens access to specialized university studies at universities of applied sciences (UAS), or in some cases, cantonal universities. In the Canton of Lucerne, institutions such as the Berufsfachschule Luzern offer integrated or post-AFC professional maturity programs.
Other apprentices continue with post-apprenticeship specializations (continuing education), international certifications in their field, or directly enter the job market with a qualified apprentice salary. Opportunities for further education depend on the individual's profile, professional interests, and access requirements for subsequent training.
### Step-by-Step Procedure: From Search to Completion
The search and application process begins about 18 months before the actual start. Consult the cantonal internship search portal, visit training fairs, and contact companies of interest directly. Prepare a CV and cover letter in line with industry expectations. The company evaluates the candidate and, if suitable, proposes a start date and details of the internship contract.
Once selected, the contract must be signed by the apprentice, parents (if a minor), and the trainer. It includes: duration, monthly salary, hours, training assignments, rights, and duties of both parties. The Canton of Lucerne's training office automatically enrolls the apprentice in the relevant vocational school (mandatory), and the company registers the apprentice with the AVS/AHV offices, unemployment insurance, and pension fund providers (if applicable).
During the internship, the apprentice regularly attends school lessons and practices in the company, completes the training journal (Ausbildungsjournal), executes practical projects, and participates in progress checks. At the end of the program, the apprentice takes a practical skills exam (at the company or cantonal exam center) and a theoretical knowledge verification (at the vocational school). Upon passing, they receive the nationally recognized professional apprentice certificate, valid as a credential in the job market.
### Practical Tools and Resources
To calculate your net salary considering mandatory social contributions (AVS/AI, AD/AC, LAINF), three-level taxation, and allowed deductions, use our [salary calculator](nav:calculator). If you want to plan your savings during the internship and understand the impact of LPP/BVG on your future pension, consult our guides on [pension and LPP](nav:pension). Finally, the internship search is a gradual and strategic process: use our [job search engine](nav:jobs) to discover open positions in the Canton of Lucerne and the rest of Switzerland, with filters for sector, duration, and location.

item.title: Apprenticeship in Lucerne: contract, salary and maturity
item.description: How to find an apprenticeship position in the Canton of Lucerne, what the apprenticeship contract must contain and how to obtain professional maturity: practical guide.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Apprenticeship: 3-4 year path between school and company - Mandatory written contract with monthly salary - Recognized diploma at the end of the path (professional maturity) - Opportunities for all professional sectors
## Key facts - **What**: Dual training system (work + vocational school) - Where: Canton of Lucerna (available in all sectors) - Duration: Typically 3-4 years - When: Usually starts after compulsory schooling - Outcome: Federal Vocational Baccalaureate (VET) or specialized diploma (CFC)
Apprenticeship represents in Switzerland one of the main professional training paths for young people. In the Canton of Lucerna, as in all Swiss cantons, the system works according to a dual model: the apprentice works in a company on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, while attending vocational school on Thursday and Friday (the proportions vary by sector).
The first step is to find a company willing to train an apprentice. Apprenticeship offers are published on national platforms, on the canton websites, and at regional professional guidance offices. In the canton of Lucerna, the Professional Guidance Office provides lists of training companies and available offers. To discover the available apprenticeship positions, consult the [job offers](nav:jobs) in your canton.
### Structure and duration of the apprenticeship
The typical duration of an apprenticeship is three or four years, depending on the sector and the chosen level of specialization. Some sectors (such as construction) provide a three-year path, while others (such as pharmacy or IT) require four years. During the apprenticeship, the apprentice follows a practical training program in the company and a theoretical program at the vocational school.
The apprentice is considered a full-fledged worker. This means that during the apprenticeship, all regulations on rest, holidays, health, and workplace safety provided by federal and cantonal legislation apply. The minimum holidays are 5 weeks per year for those under 20, and at least 4 weeks for adults. ### Apprenticeship contract and remuneration
A written contract is mandatory for every apprenticeship. The contract must specify the training company, the apprentice, the profession taught, the duration of the internship, the weekly working hours, and the monthly salary. The contracting parties must sign the document, which represents the legal basis of the training relationship.
The apprentice's remuneration varies depending on the year of training. In the first year, the monthly salary is lower; it increases progressively in the following years. These amounts are set by collective labor agreements (CCL) for sector and canton. In the Canton of Lucerne, as in other cantons, employers operating in sectors regulated by CCL must comply with the minimum salary thresholds defined by the contract itself.
In addition to the gross salary, federal social contributions apply to the apprentice's remuneration: - AVS/AI/IPG: approximately 5.3% of the salary (at the apprentice's expense) - Unemployment insurance (AD): approximately 1.1% up to an annual maximum - Accident insurance (LAINF): at the employer's expense (rate 0.7–1.5% depending on the sector)
To calculate your net salary during the apprenticeship, you can use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) which takes into account all federal and cantonal contributions of the Canton of Lucerne.
### Pension and insurance aspects
An apprentice is NOT subject to professional pension contributions (LPP/BVG) during the internship, but is once hired as an employee. The apprentice must take out health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of starting employment, choosing from the offers available in the Canton of Lucerne. Researching the most convenient health insurance fund is optional but recommended, considering that premiums vary between insurers. Many cantons offer subsidies to reduce the premium for low-income young people.
During the internship, the apprentice has the right to receive quality professional training, access to compulsory school courses, health and safety protection, and regular remuneration. The employer must provide the tools and knowledge necessary to acquire the skills provided for in the training program.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Professional maturity and diploma achievement
At the end of the apprenticeship, the apprentice must take the final exam to obtain the professional maturity diploma. This exam verifies the skills acquired both in practical business and in school education. The diploma (Federal Vocational Baccalaureate — VET, or Federal Vocational Education and Training Certificate — VET) is recognized nationally and opens the door to further continuing education paths.
After obtaining the diploma, the apprentice can directly enter the job market as a skilled worker or employee, or continue towards higher education (higher vocational school, advanced courses, master's). Those who wish to access university can attend a supplementary high school maturity.
### How to find an internship position in the Canton of Lucerne: step-by-step procedure
**Step 1: Initial research**
Visit the official internship search sites at the national and Canton of Lucerne levels. Dedicated platforms, professional association sites, and the professional orientation portal provide updated lists of companies looking for apprentices.
Step 2: Preparing the application
Write a short resume and a motivation letter showing your interest in the chosen sector. Contact the company directly to learn about the application methods. Many companies provide preliminary interviews or one or two-week 'trial internship' days to assess the suitability of the choice.
Step 3: Contract signing
Once the position is found, the employer and the apprentice sign the apprenticeship contract. The contract must be written, signed by both parties, and kept for the entire duration of the training.
Step 4: Enrollment in vocational school
The employer takes care of enrolling the apprentice in the vocational school competent for the Canton of Lucerne. This enrollment is administrative but fundamental.
Step 5: Start and progress
The apprentice starts work according to the established calendar and the school calendar of the vocational school. They attend school lessons and continue practical training in the company according to the four-year or three-year program.
To deepen the details on professional training in your canton, consult the [salary and contribution calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the net monthly salary during the apprenticeship, and check the [job offers](nav:jobs) available for new apprentices in the Canton of Lucerne.

item.title: Natural reserves put to the test by drought
item.description: The summer drought hit the swamps hard, with water levels falling to critical levels in many areas.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss wetlands have been hit by a severe drought - In some areas, the wetlands have dried up completely - Pro Natura's natural reserves have been put to the test
## Key facts - **What**: Summer drought that has affected wetlands and watercourses - When: Summer 2024 - Where: Wetland areas in Switzerland, including Rothenthurm (SZ) and Balmoos (LU) - Who: Pro Natura
This summer's heatwaves have put Swiss natural reserves to the test. The drought has particularly affected wetlands, watercourses, trees, and lakes, Pro Natura reported today.
### Effects on flora and fauna The consequences were particularly evident in the Rothenthurm (SZ) wetland area. "I have never seen the wetlands this dry since I took on the position in 2009," says Bastien Amez-Droz, project manager at Pro Natura, quoted in a statement.
The Svitto Forest Office, in collaboration with Pro Natura and some local construction companies, had carried out regeneration work to restore the water retention capacity. According to Amez-Droz, these areas remained wet at least until August, allowing dragonflies to lay eggs and newts to rest.
In the Balmoos (LU) high bog, the water level has dropped by 15-20 centimeters compared to normal. Even in this case, the worst could be avoided: "Without the renaturation work carried out last autumn, there would have been no more free water this summer," Amez-Droz continues.
In some Pro Natura natural reserves, such as in Martinet (JU), the brooks have completely dried up. In other regions, their flow has decreased, but the water has not disappeared, as in the protected areas of Gitzitobel (LU) or La Chaux-de-Brenleire, near Vanil Noir (FR).
### Impact on Ticino In Ticino, the summer heatwave has caused an exceptional proliferation of algae in the Muzzano pond. This has prevented light penetration and hindered the development of aquatic plants and animals.
"The pond suffers from an excessive load of nutrients due to the discharge of agricultural residues for several years in the past," explains Serena Britos Wiederkehr, manager of the Laghetto di Muzzano natural reserve. The excess of nutrients, particularly phosphorus, favor the proliferation of algae and cyanobacteria, a phenomenon further aggravated by the great heat, it is underlined.
Due to the unbearably high temperatures, in Ticino the pace of interventions in natural reserves has had to be slowed down, with consequent extension of the realization times, it is pointed out. ### Analysis of the effects of drought The summer drought had a significant impact on Swiss nature reserves, putting local flora and fauna at risk. Swamps, in particular, have been hit hard, with water levels falling to critical levels in many areas.
### Effects on the forest As for the state of the forests, it is very difficult to draw conclusions: only in one to five years we will see how many trees have survived, survived or are dying. Pro Natura considers the restoration of rainforests a "promising solution in the face of climate warming".
### Mitigation measures The authorities have taken several measures to mitigate the effects of the drought. These include works to regenerate marshes and peat bogs, which have made it possible to keep the areas humid and promote animal life.
### Impact on tourism The drought has also had a negative impact on tourism, with many nature reserves being closed to the public to ensure the safety of animals and plants.
### Future prospects Authorities are evaluating new strategies to address the challenges of climate change, with a particular focus on restoring natural reserves and sustainably managing water resources.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Actions to be taken To address drought, it is important to adopt water conservation and nature reserve regeneration measures. Local authorities and organisations such as Pro Natura are working to implement renaturation projects that can help restore the ecosystem.
### Tips for residents Residents are encouraged to reduce the use of water for gardening and to report any instances of swamp drainage. It is important to be aware of the importance of natural reserves and their role in the management of water resources.
### Useful tools For more information and calculation tools, you can visit our [calcolatore di imposte](nav:calculator) to get an idea of your expenses and tax obligations. In addition, you can consult the section dedicated to the [costo della vita](nav:cost-of-living) to get an idea of the daily expenses and costs of maintaining the nature reserves.
*Source: [swissinfo.ch](https://www.swissinfo.ch/ita/riserve-naturali-messe-a-dura-prova-da-siccit%c3%a0/91999663)*

item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training: Lucerne guide
item.description: How to find an internship in the Canton of Lucerne, sign an apprenticeship contract, understand the salary and achieve professional maturity.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Vocational training in Switzerland combines business teaching, vocational school and general training - Apprentice is subject to AVS/AI/IPG (5.3% employee), AD/AC (1.1%) and LAINF/LAA (0.7-1.5%) contributions - The maximum time is 45 hours per week (industry, offices, trade) or 50 hours in other sectors - Professional maturity is a federal certificate that allows access to universities of applied sciences
## Key facts - **What**: Vocational training for apprentices in Switzerland through a dual system - Who: SECO (State Secretariat for the Economy), cantons, training companies - Where: Canton of Lucerne and other Swiss cantons - When: Starts after compulsory school, generally aged 15-16 - Duration: 2-4 years according to professional address - Minimum holiday: 4 weeks per year (5 weeks if the apprentice is a minor)
Vocational training in Switzerland is one of the pillars of the national education system. At the federal level, the SECO coordinates vocational training standards, while individual cantons manage territorial enforcement. In the Canton of Lucerne, as in all Swiss cantons, apprenticeships combine three fundamental elements: practical teaching in the company (3-4 days a week), attendance at vocational school (1-2 days a week), and integrated general training (ethics, citizenship, foreign languages).
Choosing to undertake an apprenticeship is a decision In the Canton of Lucerne, as in the rest of Switzerland, finding an apprenticeship position requires personal initiative. Companies registered in the canton's list of trainers offer positions, often advertised on their websites or through sectorial trade associations (agricultural, construction, commercial, industrial, etc.). The secondary school provides information and contacts to facilitate the search for an apprenticeship.\n\n### The apprenticeship contract\n\nOnce a company willing to offer an apprenticeship is found, the apprentice and the employer sign a binding contract. The contract must specify: the total duration of the apprenticeship (2-4 years depending on the field), the monthly wage, the weekly working hours, the holiday arrangements, and the initial probationary period.\n\nSwiss law provides for an initial probationary period (generally 1-3 months) during which both parties can terminate the contract with short notice. After the probationary period, the notice periods become more stringent: 1 month in the first year, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, and 3 months from the tenth year onwards. The apprenticeship contract is regulated by federal civil law (Code of Obligations, CO), not by cantonal laws, thus ensuring national legal consistency.\n\n### Rights and protection of the apprentice\n\nDuring the apprenticeship, the young person has the right to a fair wage, although lower than that of a qualified worker in the same sector. The wage varies according to the canton, the professional sector, and the year of training: apprentices in the first year typically earn 30-60% of what an experienced professional earns; the amount increases in subsequent years.\n\nThe apprentice also benefits from fundamental rights: health and safety at work protection according to SUVA (Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund) regulations; guaranteed access to vocational school and mandatory courses; protection from discrimination. The employer, on the other hand, is obliged to provide complete and certified training, the necessary tools and raw materials, and to allow attendance at vocational school during working hours.\n\nIf you wish to check the cost of living in the Canton of Lucerne and plan your budget during your apprenticeship, [consult our cost-of-living analyzer](nav:cost-of-living).
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### The apprentice's remuneration and mandatory contributions
The apprentice's remuneration is subject to the same mandatory social security contributions as other dependent employees. Although the gross remuneration is lower than that of a qualified professional, the contributions remain unchanged in percentage.
For an apprentice, the main contributions on remuneration are: - **AVS/AI/IPG**: 5.3% on the employee's behalf (the employer pays an additional 5.3%) - Unemployment insurance (AD/AC): 1.1% up to an annual maximum - Accident insurance (LAINF/LAA): 0.7% – 1.5% depending on the industry
In the Canton of Lucerne, as in many cantons, some apprentices may be enrolled in a company pension fund (LPP/BVG) if the company provides it; this enrollment depends on the industry and the company's policy. In the first year of apprenticeship, several cantons offer partial or total exemptions from some contributions. It is important to verify with the employer and the cantonal vocational training office the specific procedures applicable to your situation.
### The professional maturity: advanced federal certificate
The professional maturity is a federal certificate that the apprentice can obtain in parallel to the apprenticeship (parallel training) or after the end of the apprenticeship (subsequent training). This certificate attests to both the specific technical skills of the trade and a solid general education (foreign languages, economics, sciences), and represents a significant added value in the labor market.
An important feature of professional maturity is that it provides direct access to university studies in applied sciences (professional universities, SUP) without an admission exam. Professional maturity requires reaching a minimum average in certain subjects. Generally, the courses are held during the last two years of the apprenticeship, 1-2 days a week in addition to the regular vocational school. In the Canton of Lucerne, as in other Swiss cantons, the canton itself and the vocational schools organize and manage the courses for professional maturity.
### Practical procedure: the steps to start an apprenticeship
1. Identify the field of interest - Choose a professional field that reflects your interests, aptitudes and career aspirations. 2. Research and applications - Consult the websites of regional employers' associations, the offers published by secondary schools, and the portals of local companies. 3. Selection interviews - Prepare a curriculum vitae and a cover letter; participate in the evaluation interviews. 4. Contract negotiation - Once you receive an apprenticeship offer, carefully examine the apprenticeship contract. Verify remuneration, weekly hours, total duration, holidays, probation period and other important details. 5. School enrollment - The employer will enroll you in the cantonal vocational school and, if desired, in the courses for professional maturity. 6. Check for benefits - In the Canton of Lucerne and other cantons, there may be cantonal subsidies for low-income apprentices, scholarships, or benefits for particular family situations. Inquire at the cantonal vocational training office.
Before signing the contract, it is essential to carefully read all the conditions. If you have doubts or questions, you can consult the Swiss workers' rights protection associations present in the canton, or directly contact the competent cantonal office.
### Tools to calculate your net remuneration
To understand the exact impact of social security contributions on your apprentice's remuneration, [you can use our payslip calculator](nav:payslip). The tool allows you to enter the gross remuneration and obtain a detailed estimate of the net remuneration, taking into account AVS, AD/AC, LAINF and other elements specific to your cantonal situation.
If you wish to deepen the functioning of the pension contributions and how they affect your future pension (whether it is AVS, LPP or the third pillar), [consult our complete guide on pensions](nav:pension). Understanding how your professional training fits into the Swiss pension system is essential for planning your financial future.

item.title: Inflation rises in Switzerland: could the SNB revise rates?
item.description: Inflation in Switzerland rose to 0.8% in August, leading to speculation about a possible change in the SNB's monetary policy.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss inflation rises to 0.8% in August - SNB may review monetary policy - Energy and franc weakness are main factors
## Key facts - **What**: Increase in Swiss inflation - When: August 2024 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Swiss National Bank (SNB) - Amount: 0.8%
The net increase in inflation recorded in Switzerland in August (0.8%, highest since September 2024) has surprised experts: now everyone is wondering if what is happening will have consequences on the monetary policy of the Swiss National Bank (SNB).
(Keystone-ATS) The majority of analysts do not appear concerned, but there are also those who believe that the institution led by Martin Schlegel will have to abandon the 0.0% level of its benchmark rate earlier than previously expected.
The progression of the parameter calculated by the Federal Statistical Office is mainly due to the increase in energy prices recorded after the failure of the truce between the United States and Iran, says Alexander Koch, analyst at Raiffeisen. "As a result, even in Switzerland, the prices of heating oil and gasoline have increased significantly."
"The increase in inflation is not really worrying," echoes Felicitas Kemeny, head of the economic sector at the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (Seco). Not least, the transport of petroleum products has become more expensive due to the low level of the Rhine. "The situation should normalize in the near future." There is no general increase in inflation, which remains comfortably within the limits of price stability: the SNB considers such stability guaranteed in a range between 0% and 2%. Several other specialists share this view. Marc Brütsch, chief economist at Swiss Life, attributes the increase in prices not only to energy prices, but also to the weakening of the franc. As a result, the costs of importing certain goods have increased. The second-impact effects on underlying inflation (that which excludes energy, fuels, fresh and seasonal products) are almost imperceptible: the relative rate rose only from 0.3% to 0.4%. “In our opinion, this does not imply any need for the SNB to act,” says Brütsch.
On the same wavelength is Santosh Brivio of Banca Migros. "The decisive question is whether the weakness of the franc leads to a lasting increase in inflation: at the current level, we believe that this risk is limited." According to Reto Cueni, chief economist of SYZ Group, the sharp increase in the prices of foreign goods, with an increase of 1.4% compared to the previous month, shows that inflation continues to come mainly from across borders: domestic prices, on the other hand, remain low. "The National Bank will carefully examine this higher-than-expected figure, but I see almost no reason why it should change its current policy."
However, there are those who do not agree: the soaring of the indicator increases the pressure on the SNB to intervene, says Thomas Gitzel, chief economist at VP Bank.

To better understand how inflation and SNB decisions can affect your economic situation, use our [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator). This tool will help you better understand the impact of changes in interest rates and inflation on your income and savings.
Also, if you want to dig deeper into the Swiss economic situation, check out our [comparatore CHF/EUR](nav:exchange) to monitor currency exchange fluctuations and understand how these can affect your investments and spending.
Finally, to stay up to date on the latest economic and financial news, subscribe to our daily newsletter. You will receive all the information you need to make informed decisions and protect your financial interests directly in your email inbox.

item.title: Working at SECO: Opportunities and Federal Career
item.description: The Secretariat of State for the Economy employs over 900 people in three locations. Discover apprenticeships, university internships and opportunities in Swiss federal public administration.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - SECO employs over 900 staff members distributed across 3 locations in Switzerland - Offers vocational apprenticeships (AFC), university internships, and specialized traineeships - Work environment that values responsibility and personal initiative
## Key facts - **What**: Employment opportunities at SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) - Where: 3 main locations in Switzerland + approximately 30 overseas detachments - Who: Federal Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs - Employees: Over 900 staff members and managers - Sought-after profiles: Commercial employees, digital business developers, IT specialists - Opportunities: Vocational apprenticeships (AFC), SMC traineeships, university internships
The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) stands as a significant employer in the Swiss federal public administration sector, with over 900 staff members and managers distributed across three main locations in the country. In addition to this national base, the federal institution has approximately 30 professionals stationed in various countries, demonstrating an active role in economic diplomacy and Swiss representation on the international stage.
For those seeking career opportunities in the federal public sector, SECO offers a concrete option: the entity provides apprenticeship positions (AFC), SMC traineeships, and university internships, in addition to traditional roles. SECO specifically seeks apprentices and young talents in three main areas. Those who enter SECO through an AFC apprenticeship or a university internship do not perform typical 'secretarial work,' but participate in assignments that require understanding market dynamics, analyzing economic data, and providing direct support to federal decisions on trade and industrial policy.

item.title: PSI researcher receives 2.2 million for quantum research
item.description: Physicist Giacomo Sala wins a European funding of 2.3 million euros for the Q-GEOMSPIN project that combines spintronics and quantum geometry. Research that could revolutionise Swiss data storage.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Giacomo Sala (PSI) receives €2.3 million (~ CHF 2.2 million) from the European Research Council - Q-GEOMSPIN project: spintronics + quantum geometry for 5 years - Since the end of 2025, Switzerland has been fully associated with EU programmes
## Key facts - **What**: Starting ERC Grant for research in quantum spintronics - When: 3 September 2026 - Where: Paul Scherrer Institut (PSI), Villigen, Aargau - Who: Giacomo Sala, experimental physicist - Amount: €2.3 million (approx. CHF 2.2 million) - Duration: 5 years - Team: 2 PhD students + 1 postdoctoral researcher
Giacomo Sala, an experimental physicist at the Neutron and Muon Research Centre of the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen, has won one of the most coveted grants from the European Research Council (ERC): a Starting Grant. The funding, amounting to 2.3 million euros — about CHF 2.2 million — will support his Q-GEOMSPIN project for the next five years. A victory that means a lot for Swiss research, especially in view of Switzerland's new full partnership with European research funding programmes, effective from the end of 2025.
What makes this initiative extraordinary? Sala combines two hitherto separate areas of research: spintronics, a discipline that has been consolidated for three decades, and quantum geometry, a young and still developing field. “As far as I know, so far no one has experimentally connected these two fields,” says Sala. ### Spintronics: from the laboratory to industrial application
Spintronics exploits the spin — the intrinsic rotation — of electrons to store and process information. The importance of this field was recognized with the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded precisely for research in this area. However, in recent years, spintronics has presented a gap that is not yet fully understood: some theoretical physics studies suggest that certain spintronic phenomena can be predicted, understood, and controlled thanks to quantum geometry, and specifically thanks to a subfield of the latter: quantum metric.
Sala uses an intriguing analogy to explain the concept. Gravity causes the Earth to orbit the Sun. According to Albert Einstein, however, the correct explanation is not a simple 'attraction' but a curvature of space caused by the mass of the Sun. 'The same applies to electrons when they move through a solid,' explains Sala. Due to quantum metric, the momentum space curves. Electrons 'perceive' this phenomenon and are consequently deflected.
### Practical applications and economic impact
Research in the Q-GEOMSPIN project could pave the way for more efficient data storage systems. In the long term, the results could contribute to the development of more powerful spintronic memories (MRAM), computer processors that operate on the model of the brain, and new material properties. It is important to note that, with the exception of giant magnetoresistance, discovered in the 1980s and which soon multiplied the storage density of computer hard drives, commercial applications of spintronics have so far been rare. Sala's project could represent a significant turning point for the Swiss and European technology industry, with employment repercussions in the high-tech sector.
### PSI as a European hub for quantum research
The fact that Sala chose the Paul Scherrer Institut for his project is not coincidental. The PSI is one of the most important research centers in Europe, with unique infrastructures and research strategies aligned with national and European priorities. In the new 'Quantum Matter and Materials Center' (QMMC) of the PSI, the work of various research groups converges in the field of quantum matter and materials. Q-GEOMSPIN fits perfectly into this new research hub, strengthening Switzerland's position in international quantum research.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Advanced infrastructures and laboratory equipment
PSI provides Sala and his team with all the necessary structures to carry out research. The team will create and measure structures of a few micrometers in size, cooled to temperatures close to absolute zero (–273.15 degrees Celsius). For this purpose, PSI acquires, thanks to ERC funds, a special cryostat: a cooling device capable of generating strong magnetic fields. Inside it, an electric current will be passed through the sample and the deviation of the electrons will be measured. In this way, researchers are looking for non-linear effects, i.e., situations where small variations in voltage or magnetic field lead to large changes in measurement.
The team will have access to three excellent infrastructures: the Swiss Light Source (SLS), the PICO cleanroom (an advanced cleanroom managed by the nanotechnology group), and the Swiss Spallation Neutron Source (SINQ). These structures are unique in Europe and allow the characterization of materials at the nanometric level. The program includes the study of topological materials (solids that are insulators inside but conduct electricity on the surface), oxide compounds, and two-dimensional Van der Waals materials such as graphene.
### Career opportunities in Swiss quantum research
With ERC funding, Sala will be able to hire two PhD students and one postdoctoral researcher. Quantum research is one of the most dynamic and growing sectors of the Swiss economy. European funding programs, now fully accessible thanks to association by the end of 2025, offer concrete career opportunities for young researchers, PhD students, and postdocs throughout Switzerland. The sector is not limited to PSI: universities such as ETH Zurich, University of Geneva, University of Bern, and other Swiss universities are heavily investing in quantum research and the training of new talents.
The skills developed in research projects like Q-GEOMSPIN — from data analysis to nanotechnology, from experimental physics to materials engineering — are highly valued in the private sector, from microelectronics companies to industrial research laboratories. A career in Swiss quantum research offers stable employment prospects and internationally competitive salaries.
### How to access funding and research opportunities
If you are a student, researcher, or recent graduate interested in a career in Swiss research, the first step is to consult the [job opportunities in the research sector](nav:jobs) and learn about the [cost of living in Switzerland and the quality of research](nav:cost-of-living) in different regions. Universities and research centers regularly publish job postings for PhD, postdoc, and staff scientist positions.
The European Research Council regularly publishes calls for Starting Grants (up to 3.75 million euros), Consolidator Grants, and Advanced Grants. The terms and application procedures can be found on the official ERC website. Thanks to Switzerland's full association by the end of 2025, Swiss researchers can also apply directly, receiving funding without institutional intermediaries.
For those who want to delve into the economic impact of salaries in the research and public sector in Switzerland, compare opportunities in different cantons and regions, and plan their career path, the [Swiss salary calculator](nav:calculator) provides a detailed overview of salaries in the research and public sector.

item.title: Bilateral III: Cantonal governments say yes
item.description: The Conference of Governments of Western Switzerland meeting in Fribourg supports the package of agreements with the EU, underlining the importance for stable access to the continental market
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Western governments support Bilaterali III in Fribourg - 7 cantons gathered at the CGSO headquarters say yes to the package - Package under review by the Federal Parliament - Update agreements to protect access to the European market
## Key facts - **What**: Bilaterali III package between Switzerland and EU - When: Today's meeting of the Conference - Where: Fribourg - Who: Governments of 7 western cantons (Berne, Fribourg, Geneva, Jura, Neuchâtel, Vaud, Valais) - Status: Under review by the Federal Parliament - Importance: Ensure long-term access to the continental market for Swiss companies
The Conference of the Governments of Western Switzerland (CGSO) gathered today in Fribourg the representatives of seven cantons—Berne, Fribourg, Geneva, Jura, Neuchâtel, Vaud and Valais—to express full support for the package of agreements between the Confederation and the European Union, known as Bilaterali III. The decision is relevant because the package is currently under review by the Federal Parliament and is considered essential to ensure Swiss companies stable access to the continental market.
### The origin of the stalemate: from 2021 to the blocking of updates
In 2021, Switzerland abandoned the negotiations on the institutional framework agreement with the EU. Since then, Brussels has refused to update several market access agreements, blocking the evolution of European legislation in the affected sectors. This situation exposes Swiss companies—in particular SMEs—to complicated procedures and additional costs to operate within the Union.
According to the CGSO, the Bilaterali III package is the concrete solution to this stalemate. It provides an official mechanism to resolve disputes between Bern and Brussels and ensures the continuation of Swiss participation in European programs such as Horizon Europe. The western cantonal governments emphasize the importance of regularly updating the agreements, not as an isolated event but as a structural process of adaptation to the continuously evolving European legislation. ### The concrete impact on Swiss companies
The lack of updated agreements directly affects Swiss companies exporting to the EU. Currently, a Swiss SME faces administrative procedures that diverge from European legislation: duplication of certifications, additional audits, longer customs clearance times. For a small to medium-sized company, these costs are significant in relation to overall turnover and operational margins.
The dispute resolution mechanism included in the Bilaterali III package is a crucial novelty compared to the status quo. So far, disputes between Bern and Brussels have been resolved slowly or not at all, blocking entire sectors and creating prolonged normative uncertainty. A defined mechanism would accelerate disputes and significantly reduce the business risk for Swiss exporters.
### Research, innovation, and global competitiveness
Access to European research programs such as Horizon Europe is not a mere administrative detail: Swiss universities, research centers, and innovative startups depend on these funds to remain competitive in the international landscape. The absence of regular participation would result in the loss of critical international collaborations, reduced access to R&D funds, and the gradual marginalization of Swiss research in the European context.
The renewal of the Bilaterali III therefore concerns not only traditional industry and commerce but the entire Swiss innovation ecosystem. The position of the CGSO is strategic: these seven cantons represent open economies, with strong exporters and established multinationals. The endorsement of the Conference signals clear political consensus among the cantonal administrations, providing a solid basis for parliamentary approval.

If you manage a Swiss company that exports to the EU or depends on European suppliers, the Bilaterali III package directly affects your competitiveness and strategic planning. Here are the operational steps to monitor and prepare.
**Monitor parliamentary timelines**: The package is under review by the Federal Parliament. You can follow the process by consulting the official communications of the Federal Council on admin.ch or the parliamentary messages on parlament.ch. Approval timelines will be publicly announced well in advance, allowing for adequate business planning.
Assess the specific impact on your sector: Not all sectors are affected equally. Manufacturing, chemical, pharmaceutical industries, and financial services will benefit most from regulatory stability. A meeting with a commercial consultant or your Swiss industry association can clarify the specific implications for your business.
Plan gradual regulatory transitions: If you currently use procedures that are not updated to EU standards, the package will mark a transition towards progressive alignment. Gather documentation on current regulatory gaps and plan compliance investments before the official entry into force.

item.title: DRY: Q2 growth, it's not boom but real
item.description: Swiss GDP +1.5% in Q2 2026. SECO slows down on boom, but enlarged growth and domestic demand recovers. Annual forecasts under review in two weeks.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss GDP +1.5% in Q2 2026 compared to Q1 - SECO: not a boom, but growth with a broad sectoral base - Annual GDP forecast (0.9%) could rise in upcoming estimates
## Key facts - **What**: Stronger-than-expected quarterly GDP growth, driven by the chemical-pharmaceutical sector - When: Second quarter 2026 - Where: Switzerland (data from the Swiss State Secretariat for Economy) - Who: SECO with economic cycle manager Felicitas Kemeny - Amount: +1.5% q-o-q; annual GDP estimate 0.9% (under review) - Leading sector: Chemical-pharmaceutical industry - Next decision: Within two weeks of the announcement
The strong growth recorded by the Swiss economy in the second quarter of 2026, with a 1.5% increase compared to the previous three months, shines a spotlight on the national economic situation. However, the Swiss State Secretariat for Economy (SECO) advises a measured assessment. Felicitas Kemeny, head of the economic cycle section at SECO, is clear: this does not represent a boom in the economy.
### Federal institution's caution
The main driver of the expansion has been the chemical-pharmaceutical industry, a historic pillar of the Swiss economy. Yet, a crucial question remains: is this truly sustainable growth, or are we simply seeing the effects of anticipation or recovery after the declines in previous months? Kemeny has not provided a definitive answer, but caution is clearly evident in the SECO's statement.
What reassures observers is the broad base of the recovery. Added value has increased in numerous other sectors beyond the chemical-pharmaceutical industry. More importantly, internal demand — household spending and private investment — has started to rise again after a weak start to the year, signaling that the dynamism is not concentrated in a single economic niche.
### Forecasts in limbo for 2026
So far, SECO economists had forecast a gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 0.9% for the entire year 2026. However, the magnitude of the quarterly surprise opens up a scenario of upward revision. SECO will communicate the new official projection within two weeks. Kemeny has openly acknowledged that "the possibility of an upward revision of the estimates is concrete".
More optimistic than Kemeny is Thomas Gitzel, chief economist at VP Bank. "This year, the Swiss economy is going quite well", declares Gitzel in a comment on the data. The expert attributes the momentum to a "surprising recovery" in European industry at this time, a trend that also benefits Swiss exporters. However, Gitzel also warns: although the strong GDP increase in Q2 is positive, "it is unlikely to be repeated with the same intensity in the short term"; growth rates will nevertheless remain "robust". ### What do these data mean for those working in Switzerland
A PIL growth that extends beyond the chemical-pharmaceutical sector has concrete reflections on the labor market and available income. When more economic sectors simultaneously record increases in added value and domestic demand rises, companies tend to invest more and hire new personnel. Switzerland, with a historically low unemployment rate, could see a further decline.
This means upward pressure on wages, particularly in secondary sectors such as construction, logistics, and commerce, which traditionally suffer less from the volatility of high-tech segments but directly benefit from the increase in consumption and private investment. An economy that grows with a broad base, as emphasized by Kemeny, is a sign that job opportunities are distributed beyond the traditional Swiss excellence niches.
### Implications for federal and cantonal taxation
Sustained economic growth increases the gross taxable income of families and employers, thereby increasing federal (direct federal tax) and cantonal revenues. Although this does not immediately result in changes in national tax rates, cantonal and municipal governments may find more room for maneuver in the 2027 and subsequent budgets.
On the other hand, growth that does not translate into structural inflation — as suggested by Kemeny's caution regarding the sustainability of rates — limits the pressure on LAMal premiums (mandatory sickness insurance). Currently, Swiss premiumists are affected by moderate annual increases; an economy that grows without overheating is the preferred scenario for federal authorities.
### What to monitor in the coming weeks
Analysts from SECO and private sector observe two critical variables: the durability of the contribution from domestic demand and the stability of the chemical-pharmaceutical sector relative to global cycles. If domestic demand does not consolidate in the following quarters, the PIL may return to annual rates around 0.9%. If, however, the recovery extends, the revision of forecasts could lead SECO to estimate an annual expansion of 1.2–1.5%.
Such a scenario would change the risk profile for real wages (income net of inflation). In a context of robust growth without rampant inflation, real wages are likely to rise, benefiting particularly employed workers in sectors driven by new demand for goods and services.

Swiss economic growth data is regularly released by SECO, which publishes seasonal economic projections on a quarterly basis. The next revision of the annual growth estimates for 2026 is expected within two weeks of the original Q2 data release, according to Felicitas Kemeny.
For those who want to monitor the national economy's performance — workers, employers, and border workers looking for occupational opportunities — it is useful to regularly consult the official SECO website (seco.admin.ch), where economic projections, economic situation press releases, and detailed data by sector are published. This practice allows for anticipating possible changes in the labor market and income scenarios.
### Important deadlines and upcoming decisions
The official SECO revision communication will take place by the first weekend of September 2026. An estimated growth of 1.2–1.5% would significantly change the available resources for federal and cantonal budgets, potentially influencing decisions on cantonal tax rates, funding for employment policies, and, in some cantons, revisions of the minimum wage.
For new workers or those renegotiating contracts, a growing economy is a strength: there is a higher probability of salary increases and better occupational conditions. Conversely, workers with short-term or interim contracts may benefit directly from a more vibrant job market, reducing the risk of occupational discontinuity in the coming quarters.

[With the arrival of new growth estimates, it's time to update your personal budget and simulate future salary scenarios.](/nav:calculator) A [salary and tax calculator](/nav:calculator) allows you to simulate how potential salary increases (a consequence of robust economic growth) will impact gross income, federal and cantonal taxation, and net available income. Similarly, [consult the cost of living tool](/nav:cost-of-living) to monitor how inflation and prices evolve in a scenario of economic growth.
Finally, for those seeking new occupational opportunities, robust economic growth is usually accompanied by a labor market recovery: [regularly consulting national job announcement portals](/nav:jobs) is a winning strategy to capitalize on expansion phases like the current one.

item.title: UBS corrects growth upwards 2026: +1.8%
item.description: UBS revises Swiss GDP 2026 from +0.7% to +1.8%. Inflation August 0.8%, estimates 2026-2027 stable at 0.6%. What changes for wages and cost of living.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- UBS revises upwards: GDP 2026 from +0.7% to +1.8% excluding sports - August inflation 0.8%, 2026-2027 estimates stable at 0.6% - Swiss economic prospects improve significantly
## Key facts
- **What**: UBS raises Swiss economic growth forecasts - When: Today, after SECO Q2 GDP data - Where: Switzerland - Who: UBS (largest Swiss bank), SECO, Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Amount: GDP +1.8% versus previous +0.7%; +2.2% with sporting events - Inflation: 0.8% in August; 0.6% expected 2026-2027
---
Zurich — UBS significantly revises upwards its forecasts for Swiss economic growth. The largest Swiss bank predicts that gross domestic product (GDP) will increase by 1.8% this year, compared to the previously estimated +0.7%. Including sports, the figure will reach +2.2%.
The announcement comes at a time of renewed confidence in the national economic cycle. The revision emerges from the analysis titled "Economic prospects improve significantly" released today by UBS following the publication of Q2 GDP data by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO). The Q2 numbers exceeded expectations, prompting the bank's analysts to recalibrate their projections upwards.
### 2027 growth slightly higher
The forecast for 2027 is also increased, albeit modestly. The estimate rises from the previous +1.4% to +1.5%. A modest but significant increase in the context of an economy accelerating compared to predictions from a few months ago.
On the price front, today's inflation data released by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) surprised UBS analysts: in August, inflation reached 0.8%. Despite this figure, the institute's experts do not foresee a fundamental change in price dynamics. Therefore, they maintain the estimate of a 0.6% increase for both 2026 and 2027. This inflation stability represents a positive element in the context of stronger-than-expected economic growth. The renewed prospects reflect a more resilient Swiss economy than initially expected, with accelerations that could have significant implications for the labor market, consumption, and federal and cantonal budget dynamics. ## What changes for Swiss residents
The upward correction of growth is not an economic abstraction, but a signal that can affect various aspects of the daily life of those residing in Switzerland. Stronger GDP growth generally goes hand in hand with a more dynamic labor market, with companies investing and hiring. In the Swiss context, where the unemployment rate is already low, an additional 0.8 percentage points of growth compared to previous estimates could translate into more competitive salaries and greater professional advancement opportunities.
At the same time, the expected inflation stability — 0.6% annually in 2026 and 2027 — represents a guarantee for purchasing power. While economic growth tends to push prices up, Swiss monetary authorities and economic actors are aiming for lasting moderation. This balance is crucial for those who depend on fixed incomes or subsidies: rents, health insurance premiums (LAMal/KVG), food, and services should remain on a predictable trajectory, without sudden shocks.
### Implications for savings and investments
For those with financial portfolios, the improvement in economic prospects can mean more favorable conditions in the markets. An expected growth of 1.8% annually — or 2.2% if the effects of major sporting events are considered — suggests that listed companies, pension funds, and investment instruments linked to the economic cycle could benefit from stronger economic fundamentals. It is not a guarantee, but a less uncertain context compared to previous projections.
It is still relevant to monitor [cost of living in your canton](nav:cost-of-living): stronger economic growth does not mean that prices remain static. Rents and services can vary by region. Even those contributing to the third pillar (3a) for pension choices might consider repositioning in light of the improved prospects. Stronger economic growth generally supports medium-term returns, although geopolitical risks remain ever-present.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to prepare: concrete actions A more positive economic outlook does not change the value of personal financial planning. On the contrary: UBS projections make it even more important to update your family budget and check fixed expenses, starting with health insurance premiums and rents.
Step 1 — Check the tax and salary impact If you receive income from employment or self-employment, economic growth could translate into salary increases. Before any contract or raise, [calculate the tax impact using our salary calculator](nav:calculator). Do not assume that a gross increase translates into an equal net increase: federal, cantonal taxes, and social security contributions (AVS/AI, LPP) significantly affect your actual paycheck.
Step 2 — Monitor health insurance premiums The expected 0.6% annual inflation does not exclude local variations in LAMal premiums. Each canton determines its own subsidy methods, and companies can adjust their rates. Check before the autumn deadline if it is worth changing insurance, especially if your income improves and you fall into a different subsidy bracket.
Step 3 — Update your annual budget With stronger growth expected, it is time to review your monthly expenses in your canton. Rents, transportation, groceries, energy: each item can move. A tool to analyze the cost of living helps you identify where your money goes and where you can optimize.
Step 4 — AVS/LPP planning and third pillar If you are nearing retirement or planning the third pillar (3a), better economic prospects reduce the risk of market crashes in the coming months. It might be time to review your LPP pension or consider new voluntary contributions. Annual growth of 1.8% creates more stable conditions for long-term decisions.
In essence: UBS's positive message is not just an abstract economic figure, but an invitation to review your financial tools and prepare to take advantage of a stronger economic climate. [Consult the salary calculator](nav:calculator) to assess the impact of any raises on your actual paycheck, thus guiding your family budget decisions in the coming months.

item.title: Digital Switzerland Committee: security and e-ID priorities
item.description: On 3 September 2026, the Advisory Committee discussed the national digital strategy, postponing the e-ID to ensure maximum security and trust.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The Digital Swiss Advisory Committee met on 3 September 2026. - Focus on digital sovereignty, security and electronic identity (e-ID). - The introduction of the e-ID has been postponed to ensure trust. - The strategy aims at a responsible and secure digital transformation.
## Key facts - **What**: Meeting of the Swiss Digital Advisory Board - When: 3 September 2026 - Where: Bern - Who: Beat Jans, Viktor Rossi, representatives of politics, cantons and economy - Objective: Security and trust in digital transformation
On September 3, 2026, the meeting of the Swiss Digital Advisory Committee was held in Bern, chaired by Federal Councillor Beat Jans with the participation of the Federal Chancellor Viktor Rossi. The event brought together leading figures from the political, scientific, economic and civil society landscape to discuss central issues related to the nation's technological evolution. At the heart of the debate, the digital sovereignty of Switzerland and the delicate dossier on electronic identity, a key tool for future access to online services. The ultimate goal, as reiterated during the work, is to allow the entire population to benefit from a digital transformation that is ecologically, economically and socially sustainable. A path that must allow citizens to move in the virtual space with maximum autonomy and self-determination. ### Error management as a development method
The Swiss strategy for digitalization adopts a critical approach to technological innovation, based on the proactive search for system failures. As highlighted by Federal Councillor Beat Jans, the e-ID program integrates preventive measures aimed at identifying weak points in the source code and optimizing the stability of the infrastructure. The use of practices such as open source, penetration testing, and bug bounty programs demonstrates a necessary willingness for transparency to build a network of trust around digital services. In a rapidly evolving technological landscape, especially due to developments in the field of artificial intelligence, security is not considered a static goal but a dynamic process that requires constant reviews. ## In a nutshell - mfe criticizes the TARDOC for not re-evaluating family medicine - Increasing outpatient costs, family medicine devalued in some cantons - Risk of removing young doctors from primary care in Switzerland
## Key facts - **What**: Criticism of the TARDOC medical tariff by Mfe - When: Communication issued by mfe (date not specified in the source) - Where: Zurich (MFE headquarters), Swiss health system - Who: Family and children's doctors Switzerland (MFE), Monika Reber and Sébastien Jotterand, co-chairs - Problem: Increased outpatient costs without re-evaluation of family medicine
The Swiss Family and Children's Medical Association (Mfe) has issued a statement critical of the TARDOC, the new medical tariff. According to the association, the introduction of this tool has not materialized the revaluation of family medicine, a goal required by every political and health party.
On the contrary, the observed picture reveals a worrying trend. The TARDOC system has led to a considerable increase in overall costs in the outpatient sector, while family medicine has even suffered a devaluation in some cantons. The only notable exception: pediatricians and general practitioners register a slight improvement in their rates.
### The persistent tariff imbalance
"Overall, the TARDOC system shows a considerable increase ### The impact on young doctors and the healthcare system
The problem goes beyond the simple economic issue. According to mfe, the tariff evolution sends a decidedly negative message to young doctors who are considering which specialty to choose. If family medicine remains economically less attractive than other specialties, with equal training and clinical responsibility, the concrete risk is that an entire generation of professionals will move away from it.
"A tariff system that disadvantages primary care so blatantly worsens the shortage of family doctors instead of combating it," says Sébastien Jotterand, co-president of the association. The shortage of family doctors is already a critical reality in many Swiss regions. To better understand how your access to primary care is ensured by the healthcare system, you can [consult the LAMal system guide](nav:health). Further professional disincentives could drastically worsen access to services for resident citizens.
### mfe's proposal: targeted, not linear corrections
mfe recognizes that, due to the general increase in costs, some tariff adjustments are inevitable to meet the cost-neutrality requirements set by the Federal Council. However, the association firmly opposes a linear devaluation that affects all medical specialties equally.
The association instead proposes differentiated and targeted tariff corrections in sectors where tariffs are truly inadequate. Specifically:
- Areas with excessive time allocations - Specialties where infrastructure and personnel costs have been underestimated
This calibrated strategy should have protected family medicine from further reductions, concentrating adjustments only where effectively necessary and justified by cost data.

TARDOC is the reference tariff for outpatient medical services in Switzerland. The established rates directly impact the costs managed by health insurance funds, which in turn influence the premiums of mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) that every resident is required to subscribe to. When overall outpatient costs increase, health insurance funds commonly pass on these increases to citizens through premium hikes.
The current situation therefore represents a multi-level challenge: on one hand, the overall costs of outpatient care have risen, which could impact premiums for all insured individuals; on the other hand, family medicine — which serves as the gateway to the system for most patients — loses economic appeal, risking a shortage of professionals that would reduce supply and lengthen waiting times.

mfe's criticisms open a broader discussion on how the Federal Council intends to address the cost-neutrality constraints without compromising the quality and accessibility of primary care. item.description: Cross-cutting motion to the Federal Council to prevent childcare abuse. The government stalls and promises a report by the end of 2027.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - National councillor calls for a national blacklist for kindergarten educators - Model for the list already exists for school teachers - Federal Council delays: report expected by the end of 2027 - Motion signed across party lines by deputies from all parties
## Key facts - **Who**: Nina Fehr Düsel (SVP/ZH), Federal Council, Swiss Parliament - What: Motion to establish a national blacklist for kindergarten staff involved in sexual abuse - When: Motion submitted; government report by the end of 2027 - Where: Bern, at the federal level - Why: Prevent educators with a history of abuse from moving between cantons without trace
Cases of sexual abuse in kindergartens have prompted Parliament to react. National Councillor Nina Fehr Düsel (SVP/Zurich) has submitted a motion asking the Federal Council to establish a national blacklist for staff in these childcare facilities, modeled after the existing list for schools.
The Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education (EDK) already maintains a list of individuals who have had their teaching license revoked due to criminal offenses, including sexual crimes. The purpose is to prevent them from working in other cantons.
### The regulatory void in kindergartens
Educators in childcare facilities do not have a similar tool. According to Fehr Düsel, a centralized list would be even more important in kindergartens: it would prevent professionals who have committed abuse from moving to another canton without trace to find new employment. Schools are promptly informed of any issues in case of multiple employments; kindergartens are not.
The motion received cross-party support from deputies of all parties, indicating widespread consensus on the issue. However, in its recently published response, the Federal Council decided to delay and rejected the motion.
The government explained that it is preparing a comprehensive report on sexual abuse committed against minors. The investigation will examine the issue in various socialization contexts, particularly in out-of-home childcare facilities, and will also assess the possibility of creating blacklists. The report will be presented by the end of 2027 at the latest.
The executive asks to wait for the results of this report before taking concrete measures. However, political pressure continues to grow: the cross-party signature of the motion suggests that the government may need to speed up the process. ### Current system: differences between schools and daycare centers
The protection of minors in Swiss educational institutions relies on established tools. The CDPE coordinates nationally the data on teachers who have lost their certification for disciplinary reasons, including sexual offenses. This system allows schools to verify the background of candidates and to communicate between Cantons to prevent the transfer of unfit personnel.
For daycare centers and childcare facilities, there is no equivalent. Verification procedures vary from Canton to Canton, and there is no national coordination. An educator who has committed abuse in one Canton could theoretically find work in another, unless the victim also files a complaint there — a scenario that exposes children to significant risks. If you are a parent looking for information on certified childcare facilities in your Canton, it is useful to delve into local regulations.
### Why the pressure is growing
The Fehr Düsel motion has been signed by parliamentarians from the right, center, left, and greens. This cross-party consensus reflects a genuine and widespread concern for the safety of childcare facilities. The Parliament, in short, has sent a clear message: the issue is not divisive, but urgent.
The Federal Council cannot easily ignore a motion so widely supported, even if it has formally rejected it. It is likely that the 2027 deadline for the report on sexual abuse will provide the opportunity to adopt concrete measures, including the creation of a national blacklist.
### What would change for the Cantons and facilities
A national blacklist would have significant administrative implications. Each Canton is responsible for the authorization and supervision of daycare centers within its territory. A centralized list would require coordination between the cantonal authorities (probably through the CDPE or a federal agency), standardized procedures for reporting abuse cases, guaranteed access to childcare facilities, and protection of personal data for those under investigation. Implementation is not immediate: it requires a legal basis, clear governance, and investments in IT infrastructure. The delay in the federal response probably reflects this complexity.

Anyone who is a parent or educator in Switzerland should not wait passively for the government report in 2027. Today it is possible to take concrete actions:
Parents. Check if your Canton has a system of certificates of good conduct ("Federal Certificate of Good Conduct") for kindergarten staff. Some Cantons already require it when signing the contract; others do not. Ask the facility directly which checks have been carried out on the background of the staff. You can contact the competent cantonal office (normally the coordination office of the reception facilities or an educational office) to report concerns. For issues related to [parental leave and family rights](nav:parental-leave), many cantonal offices offer updated guidelines.
Reception facilities. If you are managers of a kindergarten, it is advisable to adopt, from now on, stricter staff verification procedures, even in advance of national legislation. Check compliance with current cantonal laws and consider registering staff with voluntary certification systems.
Monitoring. The federal report on sexual abuse, expected by the end of December 2027, will be a milestone. It must contain concrete recommendations on the blacklist and other prevention measures. It is likely that a federal consultation with the Cantons will follow before a possible legislative change.
### Where to find information
To deepen the cantonal regulations on kindergartens, consult the competent authority of your Canton. The Federal Council will publish the report on the website of the Federal Chancellery. Interested parties (Cantons, parents' associations, educators' organizations) will have a say in the subsequent consultation.
Next step. Monitor the announcements of the Federal Council for the report expected by December 31, 2027. In the meantime, if you are involved in the world of kindergartens, check the status of the legislation in your Canton and adopt the protection measures available today.
