item.title: Apprenticeship and training Appenzello Interno: the guide
item.description: How to find an internship in the Inner Appenzell Canton, sign the apprenticeship contract, know the minimum salary, social contributions and access professional maturity.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Apprenticeship paths available in Swiss cantons for young people and adults - Apprentice contracts protected by specific federal and cantonal regulations - Apprentice wages vary by sector, with minimums set by individual cantons - Professional maturity accessible after completing VET
## Key facts - **What**: Professional training with apprenticeship in the canton - Who: Appenzell Innerrhoden cantonal administration, training companies - When: Typically a multi-year path of 3–4 years depending on the sector - Where: Appenzell Innerrhoden canton + federal training locations - Contract: Governed by arts. 344–346 of the Code of Obligations (CO) at the federal level - Final certificate: Vocational Education and Training (VET) certificate + optional professional maturity - Contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% apprentice (10.6% total with employer), AD/AC 1.1% up to the maximum
Apprenticeship is a pillar of Swiss professional training, recognized at the federal level and managed by individual cantons with specific regulations. In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, as in other cantons, those wishing to start a professional training path face three crucial practical issues: where to find a training position, how the apprentice contract works, and what salary is due.
The canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, located in northeastern Switzerland, operates under the same federal framework as every other canton: companies that hire apprentices sign a contract governed by the Code of Obligations (arts. 344–346), valid nationally. The practical modalities of training position search, minimum wage amounts, and organizational details remain the responsibility of the cantonal administration and vary between cantons.
An apprentice starting the path in the canton acquires specific rights and duties. The contract, signed between the employer and the apprentice (or parents/guardian, if a minor), establishes the duration of the training (generally 3–4 years according to the sector), the work modalities in the company, and the frequency of vocational school. Social contributions also apply to training salaries: AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% for the apprentice (the employer pays the additional 5.3%, total 10.6%), AD/AC at 1.1% up to the annual maximum, according to federal regulations.
### How to find a training position
The search for a position usually starts 12–18 months before the end of compulsory schooling. In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, as in other cantons, young people can turn to cantonal professional guidance offices, industry associations, local companies, online portals for training position searches at the cantonal and national level, and vocational schools (which maintain contacts with training companies). Once a willing employer is found, the apprentice contract is signed according to the federal model (arts. 344–346 CO), which must contain: name of employer and apprentice, total duration, professional sector, work hours and school attendance, wage amount, and start/end dates. ## # Apprentice Pay: How Calculation Works
The remuneration of an apprentice varies significantly depending on the sector and economic region. In the Inner Appenzell Canton, as in every canton, the employer is obliged to pay at least the minimum set by the cantonal rules or collective agreements of the sector where it is present. Some cantons have set specific minimum wages for apprentices; others refer to industry standards set by trade associations.
In the absence of a national federal minimum wage, each canton has autonomous fixing power. The Inner Appenzell Canton, like other cantons, uses this regulatory leverage. The exact amount of the cantonal minimum wage varies annually according to specific cantonal ordinances; it is advisable to check with the Vocational Training Office of the Inner Appenzell Canton for updated data and references to category agreements.
The same contributions of ordinary employees, proportionate to the duration of work and income, apply to the internship salary: - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% to be paid by the apprentice (the employer pays the additional 5.3%, total 10.6%) - AD/AC: 1.1% up to the annual ceiling, paid equally - Health insurance (LAMal): mandatory for all residents; the apprentice must take it out within 3 months of the start of the internship. It is private insurance at per capita premiums, cantonal and not
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step: how to start an apprenticeship in the Canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden
Phase 1: Orientation and research (12–18 months before compulsory schooling)
Contact the professional orientation office of the school or canton. In this phase, aptitudes, areas of interest, and job availability in companies are assessed. Many schools in the canton organize orientation days and company visits; participating facilitates knowledge of the local market.
Phase 2: Application and interview (6–12 months before the start)
Prepare an application dossier with CV, cover letter, school certificates. Contact training companies directly or through cantonal internship search portals. Interviews can take place at the company or via video call. It is advisable to apply to multiple positions simultaneously to increase chances.
Phase 3: Signing the contract (2–3 months before the start)
Once an agreement is reached with the employer, the apprenticeship contract is signed in duplicate. The federal model (Arts. 344–346 CO) is available from cantonal authorities or industry associations. The contract must contain all essential data: duration, sector, working hours, remuneration, school frequency.
Phase 4: School registration (weeks before the start)
Registration with the cantonal or inter-cantonal vocational school responsible for the sector. Swiss vocational schools operate on an inter-cantonal basis for many sectors; the Canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden is part of network agreements with other cantons (Appenzell Ausserrhoden, St. Gallen, Thurgau) to cover less common specializations.
Phase 5: Start of the internship (1st day)
Delivery of the contract to the cantonal vocational training office for registration. Signing of the health and safety document (SST). Start of work in the company and parallel attendance of vocational school (usually 1–2 days per week).
### Practical tools and resources
For the Canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden: the Cantonal Vocational Training Office provides information on available positions, cantonal regulations, minimum wages, partner vocational schools. Some cantons manage online databases of offers; check the official cantonal website. The SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) provides information on federal apprenticeship regulations and apprentice rights at the national level. Local industry associations provide guidance on available positions in the specific sector.
Before signing the apprenticeship contract, ensure that the duration is compatible with the desired path, the proposed remuneration is at least equal to the cantonal or sectoral minimums, the working hours (max 45–50 hours/week) and school attendance are sustainable, the terms of termination and the procedure in case of disputes are clear, the company is registered in the canton's list of training companies.
### Salary simulation and social costs
We recommend using the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the net amount of an apprenticeship salary proposal, considering AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC, cantonal and municipal taxes, LAMal contributions. Many cantons offer LAMal subsidies to low-income apprentices; the calculator helps to assess eligibility and compare salary scenarios.

item.title: Buying a house in Thurgau: taxes and mortgage
item.description: Buying property in Thurgau: tax costs, own funds required, mortgage mortgage sustainability, notary procedures and timing in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Buying a house in Switzerland involves three levels of taxes: federal, cantonal, and municipal - The canton of Thurgau has its own rates for property transfers and land registry, which vary by municipality - Own funds: at least 20% of the price (national standard), banks often require 25-30% - Mortgage sustainability assessed on gross income: installments should not exceed 33% of monthly income
## Key facts - **What**: Real estate purchase in Switzerland with taxation on three levels (federal/cantonal/municipal) - Where: Canton of Thurgau (northeast Switzerland) - Who: Resident buyers or foreigners with a residence permit - Procedure: Agreement → mortgage request → appraisal → land registry → notary → registration - Taxes applied: Transfer tax (cantonal), registration fees (municipal), notary fees (cantonal tariff) - Average duration: 60-90 days from agreement to registration
Buying a property in the canton of Thurgau requires a clear understanding of the Swiss tax structure. Like the rest of the Confederation, the tax system is divided into three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. Each canton—including Thurgau—has legislative autonomy to set rates for real estate transactions, notary fees, and municipal registration taxes.
The taxation on a real estate acquisition is not uniform across the territory. The transfer tax (applied as a property transfer tax at the cantonal level) varies significantly between cantons. In Thurgau, as in other cantons, this tax is applied to the transfer, in addition to any municipal taxes for land registration.
### The role of the bank and real estate appraisal
Before the final signing with the notary, the buyer who is financing the purchase must obtain approval from a bank or financial institution. The bank commissions an independent appraisal to estimate the property's value. If the estimated value is lower than the agreed price, the bank reduces the mortgage amount, requiring the buyer to increase their own funds.
Own funds (equity) represent the portion that the buyer must guarantee from their own pocket. The national standard is 20% of the purchase price; however, many banks require 25-30%, especially for long-term mortgages. If the own funds fall below 20%, the bank usually refuses the financing.
The bank also assesses the debt sustainability by applying a standardized national criterion: the monthly amortization installments should not exceed 33% of the buyer's gross monthly income. This constraint is applied by all major banks, regardless of the canton. ### Taxes and costs in real estate transactions
The transfer tax in the canton of Thurgau is governed by specific cantonal law. Since each canton has autonomous tax jurisdiction, the rate and calculation method differ from other cantons. In Thurgau, this tax is calculated on the sale price (or the cadastral value if higher) and represents a significant cost in the total purchase budget.
Notary fees (notary rights) are also regulated by cantonal tariffs. In Thurgau, the notary applies a tariff proportional to the value of the property, established by the cantonal notary tariff ordinance. This means that more expensive properties result in higher notary fees, according to a progressive scale.
In addition to these main costs, there are: - Registration fees with the Thurgau Land Registry (variable by municipality) - Real estate appraisal commission (calculated on the amount to be valued) - Possible cantonal real estate transfer taxes if applied in Thurgau - Consulting fees for tax or legal advice (if requested)
### Mortgage sustainability and the 33% criterion
Swiss banks apply a standardized national criterion: the monthly amortization installments must not exceed 33% of the buyer's gross monthly income. This constraint is effectively applied by all major banks, regardless of the canton.
**Illustrative example** (hypothetical, not related to specific Thurgau data): a buyer with a gross monthly income of CHF 6,000 can afford maximum installments of CHF 1,980 (corresponding to 33%). Considering an illustrative mortgage interest rate, this would allow financing a specific amount. The actual calculation depends on: - The mortgage interest rate in effect at the time of application - The chosen amortization term (15, 20, 25 years) - Any other financial burdens (personal loans, leasing)
### Tax deductions and AVS
At the federal level, passive interest on the mortgage is deductible from the taxable base of the federal direct tax. This deduction reduces the amount of taxes to be paid annually.
Regarding social security (AVS/AHV and LPP/BVG), the purchase of a property does not result in changes to the mandatory contributions. However, many buyers resort to withdrawals from the third pillar (3a) or from LPP assets to increase their own funds, according to federal regulations that allow such withdrawals in the case of purchasing the first main residence.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Step-by-step procedure in the canton of Thurgau
**1. Search and offer** — Identification of the property on the market; preparation of a written offer to the seller (usually non-binding unless otherwise specified).
2. Compromise (pre-contract) — Signing of a preliminary document that sets the agreed price, conditions, closing date (usually 60-90 days), and other clauses (e.g., financing subject to bank approval).
3. Mortgage application — The buyer submits documentation to the bank: - Identity document and residence permit (if foreign) - Bank statements for the last 3 months - Tax returns for the last 1-2 years - Pay slip or employment contract - Documentation on other debts (mortgages, loans, leasing) - Declarations of the origin of own funds (anti-money laundering regulations)
4. Property appraisal — The bank orders an independent valuation of the property from a recognized appraiser. The appraisal is decisive: if the estimated value is lower than the price, the bank reduces the mortgage.
5. Bank conditions — The bank communicates the approval of the mortgage (or the request for conditions: increase in own funds, additional documentation, etc.). These must be resolved before the notarial signature.
6. Mortgage registry check — The notary's office (or the buyer through the real estate agent) verifies with the Thurgau cantonal land registry that the seller is the legitimate owner and that there are no undisclosed mortgages, encumbrances, or seizures.
7. Signature with the Thurgau notary — Signing of the property transfer deed. At this moment: - The buyer pays the own funds - The bank credits the mortgage - Taxes on transfers, notary fees, and registration costs are settled (fully or by withholding)
8. Registration with the land registry — The notary ensures the registration of the deed with the Thurgau land registry. Only after registration is the transfer formally concluded.
### Document checklist and timelines
Essential documentation: - ✓ Seller's property certificate - ✓ Tax returns (last 1-2 years) - ✓ Bank statements (last 3 months) - ✓ Pay slip or employment contract - ✓ Documentation on other debts - ✓ Certificate of good conduct (if required by the bank) - ✓ Declaration on the origin of own funds
The average timeline from the signing of the compromise to registration is 60-90 days. The slowest factors are the mortgage application process (15-30 days), the appraisal execution (10-20 days), the resolution of bank conditions (variable), and the final coordination with the notary.
### Resources and practical calculations
To estimate the value of the transfer tax and specific notary fees for your property in Thurgau, consult the Thurgau cantonal tax office for current rates. A [mortgage calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to simulate monthly installments and debt sustainability based on the current interest rate.
Consultation with a Thurgau notary remains the safest step to understand the total tax burden specific to the property you intend to purchase. Many banks also offer free pre-consultations to estimate the maximum mortgage amount based on your income.

item.description: How to get the LAMal premium reduction in the canton of Thurgau: available deductibles, subsidy requirements and procedures to apply for the cantonal benefit.

## In brief - LAMal is mandatory for all Swiss residents within 3 months - Available deductibles: from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 per year - Premium reduction: cantonal subsidy upon annual application - Procedure: contact the competent cantonal administrative office
- **What**: Mandatory health insurance with premium reduction option - When: Enrollment within 3 months; annual subsidy application, renewal recommended before expiration - Where: Canton of Thurgau — cantonal administration - Who: Residents with income and assets within cantonal thresholds - Deductibles: CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 per year - Reduction: Based on income, assets, family composition
In the Canton of Thurgau, as in the rest of Switzerland, mandatory health insurance (LAMal, known as KVG in German) is a central aspect of the national healthcare system. Every resident is required to take out a policy with a private insurer within three months of arriving in Switzerland. Premiums vary based on several factors: the canton of residence, the region, age, gender, and the chosen coverage model. In addition to the basic premiums, residents have a crucial tool to reduce the economic burden: premium reduction, financed through a cantonal subsidy.
### LAMal in the Canton of Thurgau: structure and obligations
LAMal in Switzerland is not a contributory system funded by the employer, but a private policy with per capita premiums, taken out directly between the insured and the insurance company. Each canton, including Thurgau, sets the coverage obligation for its residents, while management remains at the private level. Premiums consist of two elements: the basic premium (monthly or annual) and the deductible. The deductible represents the amount the insured must pay out of pocket before the insurer starts covering medical expenses.
In the Canton of Thurgau, as in the rest of Switzerland, the available deductibles are CHF 300, CHF 500, CHF 1000, CHF 1500, CHF 2000, and CHF 2500 per year. A higher deductible allows for a lower monthly basic premium, and vice versa: the choice depends on personal needs and financial capacity. Those who expect few medical visits can opt for a high deductible and save on the annual premium; those with regular health needs prefer a low deductible, accepting a higher basic premium.
### Coverage models and alternatives in Thurgau
In Thurgau, several insurance companies operate with varying offers. In addition to the basic model (free choice of doctor), there are alternative models such as insurance with a mandatory primary care physician or limited access to certain hospitals and specialists. These models offer lower premiums compared to the basic model because they limit the freedom of choice and allow the insurer to better manage costs. The choice is individual: those who accept having a primary care physician or limited access benefit from significant savings on the monthly premium. Once the model and deductible are chosen, the premiums are communicated by the insurer and remain fixed until the annual contract expiration. Each year, usually between September and November, insurers communicate the new premiums for the following year, reflecting the adjustment to medical costs and market dynamics at the cantonal level. ## Cantonal subsidies: how premium reduction works
The reduction of premiums is the first tool that the Swiss system makes available to contain the economic burden of LAMal, especially for residents with modest or medium income. This is not an automatic discount by the insurer, but a cantonal subsidy provided by the Canton of Thurgau directly to the eligible resident. The subsidy is not the same for everyone: it depends on gross and net income, assets, the number of dependants and the composition of the household.
Each canton sets its own criteria and maximum subsidy amounts, based on a federal law that guarantees a minimum level of protection. In Thurgau, these criteria are defined by the competent cantonal administration, typically the Department of Health or an office dedicated to health subsidies. The federal system provides that the insured's net premium (gross premium minus subsidy) does not exceed a percentage of the net income of the household, ensuring that no one is excluded from coverage for economic reasons.
### Eligibility criteria and subsidy calculation
To obtain the premium reduction in Thurgau, the resident must comply with specific criteria related to:
- **Income**: the gross annual income must fall within a maximum threshold set by the canton, which varies according to the number of people in the household (adults, spouses, children). - Equity: Equity also
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Step-by-step procedure: how to apply for the premium reduction in Thurgau
To concretely obtain the premium reduction in Thurgau, it is necessary to follow a precise procedure. Although the application can theoretically be submitted at any time of the year, it is advisable to act before the deadline to obtain the subsidy as soon as possible and reduce the economic burden of payments.
**Step 1: Gather documentation**
Prepare all the necessary documentation before submitting the application: copy of the tax return from the previous year (or extract of taxable income), residence certificate issued by the municipality of residence, copy of the LAMal insurance policy or enrollment document with the insurer, any additional income documents (pay slips, bank statements, employment contracts), asset documentation if required, official application form for the Canton of Thurgau downloadable from the administrative portal.
Step 2: Check preliminary eligibility
Consult the website of the Thurgau cantonal administration for a quick estimate of eligibility. Many Swiss cantons offer an online calculator that allows you to enter income and family composition to obtain an estimate of the subsidy amount you are entitled to. This tool provides a first orientation and helps to evaluate whether to proceed with the formal application.
Step 3: Fill out and submit the application
Download the application form from the cantonal administration website or pick it up at the physical counter. Carefully fill out all required fields: personal data, income, assets, family composition, information on the current LAMal policy. Attach the documentation listed in Step 1. Submit the application at the counter of the competent cantonal office (Department of Health or Health Subsidies Office) or send it by registered mail or email, if the canton allows it. Always keep a copy of the application and the delivery receipt.
Step 4: Monitor processing
The cantonal office will communicate the outcome of the application in writing within 30-60 days from the receipt of the complete request. If the application is approved, you will receive communication of the subsidy amount, the method of disbursement (direct credit to the account or payment to the insurer), and the start date of the subsidized coverage.
Step 5: Mandatory annual review
The subsidy is not permanent: it must be renewed every year, following the same procedure. It is advisable to plan the renewal application before the expiration of the rights acquired in the previous year, to avoid interruptions in subsidized coverage. Many cantons send a reminder communication, but it depends on the office: do not rely on this practice. It is the resident's responsibility to monitor the deadlines.
### Practical tools and support
To deepen the costs of LAMal and compare premiums of different insurers in Thurgau, consult the [LAMal calculator](nav:health) available on this platform. For an overview of the cost of living in Switzerland and the weight of healthcare spending on the family budget, access the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living).
Calculate your annual health insurance contribution in Thurgau and find out if you are entitled to the premium reduction using our [health cost calculator](nav:calculator). Access the tool for a personalized estimate based on your income, assets, and family composition: in a few minutes, you will have a complete picture of your expenses and possible savings through the cantonal subsidy.

## Key facts - **What**: Worker rights and protections under Swiss federal law - When: Current legislation; contributions paid continuously during employment - Where: Canton of Aargau, subject to Swiss federal law - Who: Private sector employees (industry, trade, services) - Maximum hours: 45 hours/week (industry/offices/sales); 50 hours other sectors - Minimum vacations: 4 weeks annually; 5 weeks for minors under 20 - Protected leaves: Maternity 14 weeks at 80%; paternity 2 weeks
The labor market in the canton of Aargau is regulated by the Swiss federal system, which ensures uniform working conditions, protections, and rights regardless of the canton of employment. A notable feature of Swiss labor law is the absence of a federal minimum wage—a regulatory choice that allows individual cantons to set their own. In the context of Aargau, as in any other canton, wage levels are primarily determined by market dynamics, sectoral collective labor agreements, and the degree of professional training and specialization of workers.
### The federal labor law framework
The Federal Labor Law sets a maximum of 45 weekly hours for industrial sectors, administrative offices, and retail trade. Other sectors generally operate with a 50-hour weekly limit. These hourly limits apply uniformly in Aargau and throughout Switzerland, regardless of additional cantonal choices. The guaranteed minimum vacations are 4 weeks annually for adult workers, increasing to 5 weeks for those under 20. In addition to regular holidays, federal legislation provides specific protections for particular work-life situations. Maternity leave is set at 14 weeks, paid at 80% of regular salary, funded by maternity and paternity insurance (IPG). Paternity leave is guaranteed for 2 weeks. Notice periods for terminating employment follow a progressive timeline: 1 month during the first year of employment, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, and 3 months from the tenth year onwards.
### The salary contribution system
The Swiss social protection and pension system is financed through a structured system of mandatory salary contributions, deducted directly from the employee's paycheck. Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AVS) and Disability Insurance (AI) require a 5.3% contribution of the gross salary from the employee, while the employer contributes the same 5.3%, totaling 10.6%. Unemployment Insurance (AD) and Loss of Earnings Allowance (IPG) absorb an additional 1.1% of the salary, up to an annual maximum set by law. Occupational Accident Insurance (LAA) varies between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the specific risk of the activity sector. Mandatory occupational pension (LPP/BVG) involves increasing contributions with the worker's age: 7% for ages 25-34, 10% for ages 35-44, 15% for ages 45-54, and 18% for ages 55 until the retirement reference age. All these amounts are deducted directly from the gross salary and flow into federal pension funds. ## Collective agreements and wage structure
Collective labor agreements (CCL) represent the main mechanism for determining wages in various sectors of the Swiss economy, including the canton of Aargau. Where there is no federal minimum wage, these agreements — negotiated between employers' associations and trade unions — establish minimum wage levels, salary progression margins, and additional benefits for specific categories of workers. In Aargau, as in other industrialized cantons, CCLs cover a significant portion of the labor market, ensuring a certain standardization of wages even in the absence of a legally imposed minimum.
The federal contribution structure we have described — AVS, AI, AD, IPG, LAA, and LPP — represents a substantial portion of the gross salary, normally between 12% and 15% for an average worker, depending on age and sector of activity. This means that an agreed gross salary translates into a lower net pay after the deduction of these mandatory contributions. In addition to this layer of mandatory deductions, federal, cantonal, and municipal taxes are added, which vary depending on the canton of residence. The canton of Aargau applies its own tax rates at the cantonal level, to which the municipal multipliers established by the individual communes of Aargau are added. A person who works and resides in Aargau will therefore pay both federal social security contributions and cantonal and municipal taxes of Aargau.
### Wage differentials by level of education
Wage levels follow typical patterns of the Swiss economy, where the level of education is the main determinant of remuneration. A worker with a vocational certificate (AFC) typically earns less than a worker with a higher technical diploma (ITS), who in turn earns less than a university graduate. However, professional experience, technical specialization, and the specific sector of activity also significantly influence remuneration. In the manufacturing and technology sectors, traditionally strong in German-speaking Switzerland and Aargau, wages tend to be above the national Swiss average, while in retail and personal services, salaries are generally lower. Labor mobility remains a relevant aspect: a worker who changes canton may find different market conditions, even if the federal legal framework remains the same.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to navigate the Swiss system: practical procedure
For those starting to work in Aargau or changing jobs within the canton, it is essential to understand how the payslip is structured and what rights are guaranteed by federal law. First, check if your sector is covered by a collective labor agreement: most major sectors are. If so, your employer is legally obliged to respect the minimum wages and conditions set out in the CLA. This means that your salary cannot fall below the level set by the collective agreement.
Second, carefully examine the payslip you receive. You should clearly see: - The agreed gross salary - Deductions for AHV/AI (5.3% as an employee) - Deductions for AD and IPG (1.1% up to the annual maximum) - Deductions for LAA (0.7–1.5% depending on the sector) - LPP contributions (variable by age group: 7%, 10%, 15%, 18%) - Withholdings for federal direct tax and cantonal/communal taxes - The final net salary you receive monthly
If you notice discrepancies or do not recognize some items, ask for clarification from the human resources department: it is your right to fully understand your salary.
### Calculation tools and vacation rights
If you want to calculate how much you will earn net based on a proposed gross salary, you can use dedicated online tools that simulate federal and cantonal deductions specific to the canton of Aargau. Remember that health insurance premiums (LAMal) — mandatory for all residents in Switzerland — are not deducted from the payslip but paid directly to the private insurer on a monthly basis. Premiums vary depending on the insurer, the chosen deductible level (from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually), and any cantonal premium reduction subsidies. If you change jobs or cantons, remember that your vacation rights do not reset: the minimum of 4 (or 5) weeks of annual vacation is a right guaranteed by federal law, regardless of how many weeks you have used with the previous employer. If your previous employer did not grant you vacation or you terminated the relationship before using it, you are entitled to compensation.

## In brief - Permit L valid for up to 1 year for temporary work - Tied to the employer, not automatically transferable - Extension requires new SEM assessment
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term permit for non-EU/EFTA foreigners - Duration: Maximum 1 year from issuance - Where: Managed at the federal level by SEM throughout Switzerland - Who: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) - Renewal: Subject to continuous employment and market needs assessment
In Switzerland, the short-term permit L is the main federal tool for the temporary employment of foreign workers from countries outside the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). Managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), it allows working in the country for a maximum period of one year.
The permit L is aimed at workers who obtain a job offer in Switzerland and for whom the employer demonstrates that the position cannot be filled by Swiss citizens, residents with a permit B, or EU/EFTA citizens. It is not restricted to a specific canton: although the issuance is managed by the SEM, the cantonal authorities (in the case of Appenzell Innerrhoden, the cantonal immigration office) provide administrative support.
### Main features of the permit L The permit L has three key elements. First: the maximum duration is one year from the date of issuance. Second: it is tied to the employer indicated in the original application — a change of employment requires a new application to the SEM. Third: the extension is not guaranteed and depends on a new assessment of Swiss employment needs and the availability of suitable candidates in the domestic market. ### Conditions for renewal The extension of the L permit is not automatic and requires a precise procedure. The employer must submit a new application for employment to the SEM before the expiry of the current leave. The renewal is subject to three factors: continuity of employment with the same employer, demonstration that no suitable candidates are available among Swiss nationals, EU/EFTA or resident B permits, and verification of the economic situation in the relevant sector.
During the period of validity, the holder of the L permit remains subject to control by the SEM and the competent cantonal authority. Any change in employment, residential or administrative situation must be communicated promptly. An involuntary interruption of employment (dismissal, end of contract) results in the loss of the validity of the permit.
### Transition from permit L to permit B An L permit holder can apply for a B residence permit, which offers significant advantages over the L. Permit B is renewable and not tied to a single employer, ensuring greater stability and occupational freedom. The transition takes place at the joint request of the employer and evaluation of the SEM. There is no automatic entitlement; the granting depends on the continuity of the need for recruitment and the approval of the competent cantonal authority.

item.title: Permit C Internal Appenzell: requirements and application
item.description: Permanent residence in Switzerland: 10 years residence (5 EU/EFTA), integration, German language. SEM procedure, cantonal criteria and naturalisation.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Permit C = federal permanent residence, automatically renewable in Switzerland - Requirements: 10 years continuous residence (5 if EU/EFTA citizen) + economic stability - Each canton adds its own integration and language knowledge criteria - Ordinary naturalization requires permit C + another 10 years + cantonal/communal criteria
## Key facts - **What**: Permanent residence permit (category C, federal SEM) - Required residence: 10 continuous years (or 5 for EU/EFTA) - Competence: Federal State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) + cantonal migration office - Integration: Evaluated by the canton (Appenzell Innerrhoden has its own criteria) - Language: Generally Swiss German knowledge at level A2/B1 required - Renewal: Automatic every 10 years (unlike permit B) - Documents: Passport, certificate of good conduct, employment contract, proof of residence
The permanent residence permit, category C, represents the permanent residence status in Switzerland for foreigners. Unlike the B permit (residence), which requires periodic renewals, the C permit renews automatically and is the first legal step towards ordinary Swiss naturalization.
To obtain it at the federal level, the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) requires a continuous period of residence of 10 years in Switzerland. Citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) benefit from a reduced term: only 5 years. However, the mere passage of time is not sufficient. Each Swiss canton — including Appenzell Innerrhoden — has developed additional integration and language knowledge criteria that the applicant must meet. These criteria vary significantly between the 26 cantons and are managed by the respective cantonal migration offices.
### Federal and cantonal requirements compared
At the federal level, the SEM and the Federal Council have defined the basic regulatory framework: years of residence, compliance with Swiss criminal laws, absence of threats to public order. At the cantonal level, the migration office of Appenzell Innerrhoden sets specific integration requirements for the territory. What does this mean concretely? The office evaluates whether the applicant for the C permit demonstrates stable ties with the territory: permanent employment or self-employment, stable housing situation, participation in the local community, possibly family. Essential is the respect for public order and local laws.
Language knowledge does not have a uniform federal standard; each canton has autonomy. In Appenzell Innerrhoden, generally a level A2/B1 of Swiss German (reading, conversation, comprehension) is required, verified through an informal interview at the migration office or through a formal test. This level does not equate to an academic certification but allows basic communication with authorities and in daily life. ### Integration: how the cantons evaluate it
Integration is not a vague concept. When the migration office of Appenzello Interno receives an application for a C permit, it concretely examines some elements. First: economic stability. Does the person have a permanent employment contract or a consolidated self-employed activity? Do you have enough income to support yourself without social assistance? Second element: family and social ties. Do you have a family permanently resident in the canton? Do you participate in associations, local initiatives, religious communities, sports clubs? Third: communication skills and compliance with the law. During the interview with the migration office, does the person demonstrate understanding of administrative instructions in Swiss German? Do you have a criminal record, labor law violations, building code violations, or other significant infractions?
There is no numerical grid: the office evaluates the set of factors. In Inner Appenzell, assessment is less formalised than in larger cantons (such as Zurich or Bern), where standardised language tests have sometimes been developed. Appenzello Interno applies semi-structured interviews and a holistic assessment. This means that two people with identical years of residence and the same income could receive different answers if one clearly demonstrates local integration and the other does not.
### From permit C to ordinary naturalization: the path
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to submit the C permit application: step-by-step procedure
Step 1: Preparation and collection of documents
Before contacting the Appenzell Innerrhoden migration office, ensure you have completed 10 years (or 5 if EU/EFTA) of continuous residence. Gather the required documents: a valid and readable passport or national ID, a certificate of good conduct and police record (available from your current canton of residence), employment contracts and the last three pay slips to prove economic stability, a copy of your lease agreement and proof of rent payments, and certificates of participation in language or integration courses if available.
Step 2: Submitting the application to the cantonal office
The application is submitted to the migration office (Migrationsbehörde) of the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden. In Switzerland, there is no single online procedure; each canton has its own system. You can fill out a paper form or a digital form according to the cantonal office's instructions. The form asks for personal data, residence history, work information, family situation, and any legal records.
Step 3: Evaluation by the cantonal office
The office will review your documents and conduct an interview (usually in person). During the interview, you will demonstrate your knowledge of Swiss German through direct conversation (no official test is required, but you must be able to understand instructions and answer basic questions). The office will also assess your integration and economic stability according to local criteria. The average time for this phase is 2-3 months, although times may vary.
Step 4: Transmission to the federal SEM and issuance of the C permit
Once the cantonal office approves the application, the file is forwarded to the federal State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). The SEM performs a final administrative check (security checks, federal databases) and, in the absence of obstacles, issues the official C permit. The permit is a plastic document that you will receive by mail. From that moment, you are "domiciled" in Switzerland, and the permit is automatically renewed every 10 years.
### Practical tools and contact information
To understand the overall impact of your economic and tax situation once you obtain the C permit, we recommend using [the salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator), which provides a personalized simulation of federal and cantonal tax obligations. Remember also that residing in Switzerland requires you to take out [mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG)](nav:health) within three months of arrival; medical coverage is a criterion for integration assessment.

Permit Reception: Once approved, the B residence permit is renewed and delivered to the applicant.
### Tools and Resources To facilitate the renewal process, various tools and resources are available. The cantonal migration office offers guides and online support, while the website of the Canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden provides detailed information on requirements and procedures. You can contact the office to obtain clarifications and assistance during the process.

This tool provides a detailed overview of the requirements and procedures, ensuring transparent and uniform management of the residence permit in Switzerland.

item.title: Wages and the labour market in Appenzello Esterno
item.description: Comprehensive analysis: salaries by level of training, hiring sectors, collective agreements, worker protections and minimum wage in the Swiss cantons.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - There is no federal minimum wage; some cantons have local regulations - Salaries vary by education, sector, experience, and canton of work - AVS/AI/IPG contributions: 5.3% of the employee's gross salary - Mandatory LPP from 17–25 years: 7% to 18% depending on age
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss salary structure varies by canton, sector, education level - Where: Switzerland (each canton has different local regulations) - Who: SECO oversees federal labor regulations; UST/BFS publishes salary data - Maximum hours: 45 hours per week (industry, offices, sales) or 50 hours (other sectors) - Minimum vacation: 4 weeks per year; 5 for those under 20 - Maternity: 14 weeks at 80% through IPG; paternity 2 weeks - Notice period: 1 month (first year), 2 months (years 2–9), 3 months (from year 10)
In Switzerland, there is no federal minimum wage. However, the situation varies significantly from canton to canton: some have introduced their own local regulations, reflecting the specific cost of living in each region. The salary structure depends on multiple factors: the worker's level of education, the sector of activity, professional experience, and especially the canton of work.
Regarding education, salary levels generally follow a progression: those with only lower secondary education earn less than those who have completed an apprenticeship (AFC), who in turn earn less than those with tertiary education (university, polytechnic, higher specialized school). This progression is not rigid but represents a general trend in the Swiss job market.
Sectors of activity are a decisive element. Banking, insurance, and technology tend to offer salaries above the national average, while retail, hospitality, and agriculture generally present more modest wages. Professional experience still counts: a new graduate with a diploma receives a lower salary than someone who has accumulated ten years of experience in the same role.
Regarding worker protections, federal labor law sets a maximum of 45 hours per week for industry, offices, and sales; other sectors may allow up to 50 hours. The minimum vacation is four weeks per year (five for employees under 20). Maternity is covered for fourteen weeks at 80% through the loss of earnings compensation (IPG), while paternity provides two weeks.
### Collective agreements and sectoral protections
Many Swiss sectors operate under collective agreements (CCS), negotiated between unions and employers' associations. These agreements define sectoral minimum wages, hours, holidays, and other benefits. Not all sectors have a CCS; in such cases, working conditions are regulated by the individual contract and federal labor law. Notice periods vary: one, two, or three months depending on the length of service, with shorter terms in the early years of employment and longer terms after a decade. How are gross and net salaries calculated? A gross salary is the total amount agreed upon between the employer and the employee, from which social security contributions and taxes are deducted. The employee contributes 5.3% of the gross salary to AVS/AI/IPG (old-age, disability, and loss of earnings insurance), plus 1.1% up to an annual maximum for unemployment insurance (AD/AC), and 0.7–1.5% for accident insurance (LAINF/LAA), the amount of which varies by sector. The employer also pays their own 50% of the AVS/AI/IPG contributions.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). How to find out about salaries in your sector and canton? The first step is to consult official sources. The Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) regularly publishes data on median salaries by sector, level of education, and region. The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) provides information on federal labor regulations, including details on working hours, vacations, and protections. The competent cantonal administration (labor office or human resources department) has data on local average salaries and any cantonal minimum wages.

item.title: Registering a business in external Appenzello
item.description: Guide to the steps, legal forms, registration costs and insurance obligations for those who open a business in canton AR.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Three legal forms: sole proprietorship, partnerships and corporations - Registration in the cantonal commercial register; cantonal and municipal taxes - Mandatory AVS/AI from CHF 2,300 income; contributions 5.3% and 10.6%
## Key facts - What: Registration of a company in the Swiss commercial register - When: Within 14 days of the company's foundation (mandatory) - Where: Commercial register of the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden - Who: Natural and legal persons exercising commercial activities - Legal forms: Sole proprietorship, general partnership, limited partnership, corporation, LLC - Federal competence: SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) - Cantonal competence: Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden for cantonal-municipal taxes
Anyone wishing to start a business in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden must first choose the legal form that best suits their situation. Switzerland recognizes three main categories: the sole proprietorship (one person managing the business), partnerships (two or more partners with joint and several liability), and corporations (corporation and limited liability company, with liability limited to the capital contributed).
Registration in the commercial register is mandatory for anyone exercising a commercial activity in a professional and lasting manner. The deadline is 14 days from the date of foundation. Without registration, the company cannot operate legally in any Swiss canton.
### Legal forms and requirements
The sole proprietorship is the simplest form: a natural person exercises the activity on their own, with full personal liability for debts. It does not require a minimum capital. The entrepreneur has full discretion over operational choices but is personally liable with their assets for any obligation of the company.
Partnerships (general partnership and limited partnership) involve at least two partners with joint liability. They are suitable for partnerships where partners wish to actively participate in management. Managing partners are jointly and severally liable with their assets.
Corporations (corporation and limited liability company) separate personal liability from business debts. A corporation requires a minimum capital of CHF 100,000, while a limited liability company requires CHF 20,000. Partners are liable only to the extent of their contributed share.
Each form entails different administrative and tax obligations. The sole proprietorship, although the simplest, exposes the owner to unlimited personal risks. Corporations offer asset protection but require greater administrative and accounting complexity.
In the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, as throughout Switzerland, the federal direct tax is levied at three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. Each canton sets its own rates and multipliers. The municipal multiplier is applied to the cantonal tax, creating significant variations between different municipalities within the same canton.
Registration in the commercial register generates the obligation to keep regular accounting (for companies) or simplified accounting (for sole proprietorships below certain volumes). The accounting must be kept for at least 10 years. ### Registration costs and taxes
The costs of registering with the commercial register vary from canton to canton. In Switzerland, there is no single federal rate: each canton and each municipality sets its own registration fees (first-time registration fee) and subsequent business taxes. This multiplicity of tax regimes reflects the Swiss federal system, where direct tax competencies are largely delegated to the cantons and municipalities.
The federal direct tax (FDT) applies at the federal level with progressive rates. To this is added the cantonal tax, the amount of which depends on the income and capital of the company. The canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, like every canton, has its own municipal multipliers that modify the cantonal rate for the municipalities of the territory.
A company generating income for the first time must take into account three levels of taxation: federal, cantonal, and municipal. The cantonal and municipal tax return must be filed together with the federal return within the set deadlines. For natural persons in the form of a sole proprietorship, the company's income is added to the personal income and taxed in the overall personal return.
### VAT and accounting obligations
If the annual turnover reaches or exceeds CHF 100,000, VAT (Value Added Tax) registration becomes mandatory. The Federal Customs Administration (FCA) manages the Swiss VAT register. Up to this threshold, registration remains optional but is recommended if the company has significant deductible costs or intends to export services abroad.
Every company is obliged to issue invoices, keep the original accounting documentation, and maintain accounting records. Sole proprietorships below the VAT limit can adopt simplified accounting (minimum ledger), while corporations must comply with ordinary accounting standards (full income statement, balance sheet). All registers, invoices, and supporting documents must be kept for at least 10 years from the last movement.
### Capital tax and social contributions
In addition to income tax, capital companies may be subject to a capital tax (normally in public limited companies). The level and rate depend on the canton: Appenzell Ausserrhoden, like every canton, applies its own rules to the capital funds.
The company must also distinguish between initial setup costs (notary for drafting the deed, registration with the commercial register, application for a company AHV number with the tax office) and recurring annual costs (registration fees, income and capital taxes, social security and insurance contributions, accounting). There is no universal amount: a craft sole proprietorship has lower startup costs than a corporation with professional creditors. With the [tax calculator](nav:calculator), you can estimate the tax burden of your company depending on the legal form and canton. The only certainty is that the commercial register issues a registration certificate, essential for operating legally and opening business bank accounts.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Insurance and Pension Obligations
Every entrepreneur and every employee must be insured with the Old Age and Survivors' Insurance (AHV) and the Disability Insurance (IV). The obligation arises for a net income from gainful employment of at least CHF 2,300 annually. The contributions are 5.3% for the employee and 10.6% in total for the employer (based on the salary mass). For self-employed individuals (sole proprietorships), the payment is 10.6% based on the net income.
In addition to AHV/IV, contributions to unemployment insurance (ALV) and accident insurance (UVG/UVG) are mandatory. ALV amounts to 1.1% up to an annual maximum set by law, while UVG/UVG varies from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector of activity (agriculture, industry, offices, sales, healthcare, etc.). The canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, like all others, applies these federal rates.
For employees, the contribution to the pension fund (BVG, occupational pension fund — mandatory from CHF 21,330 of coordinated salary) depends on age: 7% for 25-34 years, 10% for 35-44, 15% for 45-54, and 18% for 55+ until the reference age. These amounts apply to the so-called 'coordinated salary mass', i.e., the gross salary minus the coordination deduction. With [AHV and BVG](nav:pension) you can calculate your benefits and understand how they evolve over time.
Those residing in Switzerland (including entrepreneurs and employees) must take out health insurance (KVG, Federal Law on Health Insurance) within 3 months of arrival in the country. It is a private insurance with per capita premiums, NOT a tax or a deductible salary contribution. Each person, regardless of income, chooses their own policy among the authorized insurers.
Premiums vary according to canton, region, age, and chosen deductible. Deductibles for adults range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually; each canton offers premium reductions (cantonal subsidies) for those with low income, based on declared income and assets.
In the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, health insurance is administered at the cantonal-municipal level, but the choice of policy remains individual: no centralized public insurer, but a private market with competition among federally recognized health insurance funds (health insurance-accident insurance and optional supplementary insurance).
### Step-by-Step Procedure
1. Choose the legal form (sole proprietorship, company, etc.) based on the project and asset protection needs 2. Register with the cantonal commercial register within 14 days of founding 3. Obtain the company AHV identification number (from the cantonal tax office) 4. Register with the occupational pension fund (BVG) if you have employees 5. Enroll in health insurance within 3 months of residence in Switzerland 6. Open a business bank account with the registration certificate 7. Submit the first federal-cantonal-municipal tax return within the legal deadlines
The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) provides information on the rights and obligations of entrepreneurs at the federal level. For specific details on communal and cantonal taxes in Appenzell Ausserrhoden, contact the cantonal tax office or the municipal offices in your area of operation.

item.title: Open activities in Appenzello Externo: costs
item.description: Registration in the trade register: legal forms, tax obligations, AVS/AI and LAMal contributions. Practical guide to Appenzello Esterno.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Registration in the commercial register is mandatory for all Swiss companies (sole proprietorship or corporation). - Basic documents: copy of ID, registration application, proof of residence, civil registry extract. - After registration, AVS/AI/IPG contributions apply (5.3% employee, 10.6% total with employer). - LAMal is mandatory for all residents; premiums calculated per capita per canton.
## Key facts - **What**: Registration of activity in the Swiss commercial register - When: Before starting the activity; single federal procedure in Switzerland - Where: At the cantonal commercial register office (each canton has its own) - Who: Sole proprietorships, Snc, Sagl, Sa, cooperatives - Requirements: ID, residence, legitimacy, official registration form - Contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employees (10.6% total with employer) - Insurance: LAMal mandatory, LAINF/LAA (0.7–1.5% sector), LPP if coordinated
Anyone wishing to start a business in Switzerland — including in the Canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden — must first understand the federal registration obligations, the legal form constraints, and the tax and contribution implications. The registration procedure in the commercial register is identical throughout Switzerland: it is a federal registration, although managed at the cantonal level through the official office of the canton of residence of the company.
Whatever legal form is chosen — sole proprietorship, simple company, collective name company (Snc), limited liability company (Sagl), public limited company (Sa) — the company cannot operate without registration in the commercial register (RDC). This is a federal legal obligation, not optional.
### What is the Swiss commercial register
The commercial register (RDC) is the public register that records all companies that carry out an organized economic activity in Switzerland. Each canton manages its own office, but the data flows into a single federal register managed by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (Seco). Registration creates a public file containing: company name, legal form, address, legal representatives, share capital (if required). Anyone can consult the RDC online to verify the existence and data of a company.
To register, the entrepreneur (or founding partners) must submit: registration application on the official form, copy of ID (passport, Swiss ID card, residence permit for foreigners), recent proof of residence, civil registry extract, constitutive documents of the company (notarial deed or statutes, if a company). The procedure is electronic in many cantons, paper-based in others, or mixed. There is no uniform federal cost: each canton sets its own registration fees. Once registered, the entrepreneur enters the federal tax system and must comply with VAT declaration obligations (if turnover ≥CHF 100,000/year), federal direct tax, and cantonal/communal taxes. ### Available legal forms
In Switzerland, there is no single "business model". The choice of legal form depends on the number of partners, available capital, desired personal liability, and acceptable administrative burden.
**Sole proprietorship**: A single natural person exercises the activity under their name. The responsible person is personally and unlimitedly liable for debts. No minimum capital is required. It is the simplest and least costly form, but it fully exposes personal assets to business risks.
General partnership (Snc): Two or more associated persons. Each partner is personally and jointly liable for the company's debts. Requires a conventional minimum capital. Rarely used for modern commercial enterprises.
Limited liability company (Sagl): One or more partners. Liability is limited to the paid-in capital, not personal assets. Requires CHF 20,000 minimum capital. It is the preferred form for SMEs in Switzerland for the balance between limited liability and administrative simplicity.
Corporation (Sa): One or more shareholders. Liability is limited to the paid-in capital. Requires CHF 100,000 minimum capital (CHF 50,000 if named shares). Heavier administrative structure, with shareholder meetings and boards of directors. Suitable for large enterprises or for institutional credibility needs.
Cooperatives: Association of persons with a mutualistic purpose. Limited liability. Rarely used in the context of business start-ups, more common in agriculture and collective services.
### Initial tax obligations
Immediately after registration in the RDC, the company becomes subject to taxation at three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. Federal direct tax (IFD): Applied to the company's net income. Rates vary by canton, but the system is progressive and centrally managed. Value-added tax (VAT): Mandatory if annual turnover exceeds CHF 100,000. Below this threshold, registration is optional. The standard rate is 7.7%, with reduced rates for food and media (2.5%). To estimate your overall tax burden, consult the [tax calculator](nav:calculator). Management requires quarterly or annual declarations to the Federal Customs Administration (Aduc).
Cantonal and municipal taxes: Each canton (in this case, Appenzell Ausserrhoden) sets its own rates on income and capital. The cumulative cantonal + municipal burden creates the overall tax burden. There is no uniform value: cantonal autonomy is absolute. The registered company must register with the cantonal/municipal tax administration within the prescribed deadlines to avoid penalties.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Social contributions and mandatory insurances
The employer who hires employees (or who is an employee of a company that is being founded) incurs federal contribution obligations. **AVS/AI/IPG** (old-age/invalidity/loss of earnings compensation): The employee pays 5.3% of the gross salary. The employer pays an additional 5.3%, for a total of 10.6%. This is one of the most significant burdens for an SME.
Unemployment insurance (AD) and Disaster insurance (AC): Payment of 1.1% up to an annual maximum, regardless of the canton.
Accident insurance (LAINF) and Occupational illness insurance (LAA): Vary by sector (0.7–1.5% of the coordinated salary). Construction, manufacturing, and agricultural companies have higher rates; offices and commerce have lower rates.
Professional pension (LPP/BVG): Mandatory if the coordinated salary exceeds the threshold (currently approximately CHF 22,050 per year; amount indexed annually). The employee pays from 7% to 18% of the coordinated salary, depending on age (7% at 25–34 years, 10% at 35–44, 15% at 45–54, 18% at 55 years until the reference age).
LAMal (mandatory health insurance): Every resident in Switzerland must take out health insurance within three months of arrival. It is not a tax, but a private insurance with per capita premiums, which vary by canton and deductible class. Consult the health insurance comparison tool to evaluate LAMal premiums in your canton of residence. Deductibles for adults range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually. The canton can provide premium reduction subsidies to low-income residents.
### Step-by-step: how to start the activity
1. Decide the legal form (sole proprietorship, GmbH, AG) based on the number of partners and available capital.
2. Gather the basic documents: copy of ID, proof of residence, civil registry extract, articles of association or deed of incorporation (if a company).
3. Register with the cantonal commercial register office (Appenzell Ausserrhoden: State Chancellery of the canton). Electronic or paper operation depending on the canton.
4. Registration in the federal commercial register: Automatic after cantonal approval.
5. Registration with the cantonal/communal tax administration: Paper or online forms; varying deadlines.
6. Registration as an employer with AVS/AI compensation funds: Necessary if hiring personnel.
7. Take out mandatory insurances: LAMal within 3 months (residents); LAINF/LAA through the employer; LPP if necessary.
8. Open a business bank account: Not legally required, but recommended for tax transparency.
Once these steps are completed, the company is operational and compliant with federal, cantonal, and communal regulations. Consult the website of the commercial register office of the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden for opening hours, official forms, and specific cantonal costs. Calculate the overall tax burden using the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) to adequately plan the start of your activity.

item.title: Rentals Zurich: rental rights and procedures
item.description: Complete guide to the right to rent in the Canton of Zurich: security deposit, chargeback, cancellation and legal deadlines.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Maximum security deposit 3 months' rent (Code of Obligations art. 257c) - Blocked account in the tenant's name for money protection - Rent dispute within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Termination only valid on official cantonal form
## Key facts - **What**: Federal rental rules (Code of Obligations, art. 253 ff.) - Where: Canton of Zurich (same law throughout Switzerland) - Who: Tenant, landlord, cantonal conciliation authority - Maximum deposit: 3 months' rent - Rent dispute: Within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Termination: Official cantonal form with legal terms (1/2/3 months) - Legal framework: Federal, identical application in all cantons
### The national legal framework In the Canton of Zurich, as in all of Switzerland, rental law is governed by the Code of Obligations at the federal level. The rules on the security deposit, the dispute of the initial rent, and the termination procedure are identical in every canton: a tenant in Zurich has the same rights as one in Lucerne, Graubünden, or Ticino. Knowing these rules in advance helps those looking for an apartment in the largest region of German-speaking Switzerland to protect themselves from the moment of signing the contract.
The security deposit (Kaution in German) is the first financial hurdle for those renting a home. Federal law sets an absolute maximum limit: 3 months' rent. A landlord who requests a higher amount commits an abuse of rights. The money must be deposited in a blocked account (Sperrkonto) in the tenant's name and not the landlord's: this legal protection ensures that the money remains safe and recoverable at the end of the lease.
### Termination: form and deadlines Termination is a second critical point often underestimated by tenants. It is not enough to send an email or an informal letter to the landlord. The law requires the official form of the Canton of Zurich for the termination of a lease, available from the conciliation office, the municipality of residence, or the district. This formality is not mere bureaucracy: it serves to avoid legal disputes over whether the termination was properly notified and within the correct deadline.
Termination deadlines vary depending on the length of the contract. During the first year, the deadline is 1 month for both parties (landlord and tenant). From the second to the ninth year, the deadline increases to 2 months. From the tenth year onwards, the deadline becomes 3 months. If the contract does not specify otherwise, these legal deadlines apply automatically. A termination submitted outside the deadline is null and void.
### Protection of the security deposit at the end of the lease An often overlooked aspect concerns the guarantees on the deposit at the end of the contract. If the landlord keeps the money in their own current account mixed with their funds, the tenant risks not being able to recover the money in case of the landlord's insolvency. For this reason, the Code of Obligations prescribes the blocked account, a legally guaranteed form of deposit. At the time of signing the contract, the landlord must provide a document (bank statement, letter from the bank) that proves where the deposit is deposited. If the landlord omits this communication, they have violated a legal obligation.
At the end of the lease, the landlord has 30 days to return the deposit. If they withhold amounts for alleged cleaning costs, repairs, or damages, they must justify each deduction with specific documentation (quotes, invoices). If the tenant believes that the deductions are unjustified or excessive, they can [check the overall cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) and possibly dispute it with the conciliation authority. ### How to contest the initial rent
When the tenant signs the lease agreement, they accept the monthly rent proposed by the landlord. However, federal law provides an escape clause: if the rent is disproportionately high compared to market rents in the area and the characteristics of the property, the tenant can contest it. The contestation must be submitted within 30 days of signing the contract to the conciliation authority of the Canton of Zurich.
The 30-day deadline is strict and non-negotiable. After these days, the right to contest expires automatically, and the rent becomes final. The date that counts is the date of receipt of the appeal at the conciliation authority, not the date of sending. For this reason, sending the appeal by registered mail is strongly recommended: it provides proof of the sending date.
The evaluation of the rent is not subjective. The conciliation authority compares the contested rent with the rents practiced for similar leases in the same geographical area. It analyzes objective factors: square footage, number of rooms, precise location, year of construction, amenities (heating, elevator, garden, parking, basement), state of the property, history of previous rents of the same unit. If the rent is indeed excessive compared to these parameters, the authority can oblige the landlord to reduce it retroactively from the first month of the lease.
### The procedure at the conciliation authority
The conciliation authority is a cantonal administrative body present in every district or municipality of the Canton of Zurich. Zurich city, Winterthur, and other major municipalities have their own offices; smaller municipalities refer to the district office of territorial competence.
The tenant wishing to contest the rent must submit a written appeal form (Rekurs) to the competent office, attaching: - A complete copy of the signed lease agreement - Documentation of payments made (bank transfers, checks, bank statements) - A detailed description of the property's characteristics (number of rooms, total square footage, type of heating, elevator yes/no, garden, parking, state of conservation) - If available, a comparison with rents of similar properties in the same area (screenshots of real estate ads, data from agencies, specialized sites)
The authority summons the landlord and the tenant to a conciliation hearing. The main objective is to reach an amicable agreement. Both parties can present new evidence and counterarguments. If no agreement is reached, the authority issues a reasoned opinion (Schiedsspruch) specifying what the fair rent should be based on local market data. This opinion is not yet a judicial sentence but is factually binding: the landlord who refuses the opinion risks being reported to the civil court by the tenant.
### Distinction between security deposit and rent
A frequent confusion among tenants concerns the substantial difference between security deposit and rent. The deposit is a single sum that the tenant pays at the time of signing the contract as a guarantee for the landlord. This sum remains unchanged for the entire duration of the lease and is returned at the end, except for legitimate deductions for documented damages or expenses. The rent, on the other hand, is the recurring monthly payment that the tenant pays each month to use the property.
Contesting the security deposit makes no legal sense: the Code of Obligations sets the maximum at 3 months' rent, and there is no room for negotiation on this amount. Contesting the monthly rent, however, is a concrete legal procedure. The conciliation authority can declare the rent unfair and obtain its reduction retroactively from the first month of occupancy of the property. This distinction is crucial for a correct strategy to protect rights.
### Timeline of the contestation
After the submission of the appeal, the conciliation office verifies the formal requirements. If the appeal is complete and submitted on time, it proceeds with the summons. Usually, 2-4 weeks pass before the date of the hearing. The hearing itself lasts on average 30-60 minutes. If there is no agreement, the authority will issue the opinion within a further period (usually 2-3 weeks). The opinion is notified in writing to both parties.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). # ## Step-by-step procedure for the tenant If you have signed a lease in the Canton of Zurich and believe that the monthly fee is unfair compared to the local market fees, here are the concrete steps: Step 1 – Check the deadline: You have 30 days from the signing of the contract to file an appeal. This term is mandatory: it cannot be extended. The date that counts is the date of receipt of the appeal with the conciliation authority, not the date of dispatch. Count the days carefully. Step 2 – Collect all the documentation: Photocopy the original lease, payment forms (bank transfers, checks), payment receipts. Document the physical characteristics of the property (number of rooms, size, heating, elevator, parking). If you know of rentals of other similar homes in the area (through online ads, real estate agencies, specialized sites), keep screenshots with date and source. Step 3 – Identify the relevant office: Contact the municipality of your residence or the relevant district of Zurich. Ask for the address and time of the conciliation office (Vermittlungsstelle, Conciliation). Many offices have websites where you can download the appeal form (Rekurs). Step 4 – Fill out the appeal: Use the official form. Complex legal drafting is not necessary. Explain clearly and briefly why you feel the fee is excessive. Attach all original documentation or certified photocopies. Investing 30-45 minutes of prior attention in the correct preparation of the appeal is much more convenient than facing months of legal disputes. If you have any questions about the procedure, please contact the conciliation office directly: operators can provide free and impartial assistance.

item.title: New US duties on Swiss goods: what changes from 2026
item.description: From 24 July 2026, the United States will apply variable tariffs of up to 12.5% on Swiss goods. SECO monitors the implications for businesses.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - US tariffs on Swiss goods from July 24, 2026 - Additional tariff up to 12.5% - Free trade agreements optimized on August 20, 2026
## Key facts - **What**: New US trade tariffs - When: July 24, 2026 - Where: United States / Switzerland - Who: SECO - Amount: 12.5%
On July 24, 2026, the United States introduced new tariff measures in the form of additional duties following an investigation conducted under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974. This investigation specifically focused on the trade of goods produced using forced labor. For imports from Switzerland, an additional tariff has been established, which can reach a maximum rate of 12.5%. It is understood that in calculating this imposition, the existing MFN (Most Favored Nation) tariffs between the parties will also be taken into account. The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) continuously monitors the evolution of these international dynamics that directly impact Swiss trade. Following these measures, a turning point was reached in bilateral negotiations: on August 20, 2026, the negotiations for the optimization of the free trade agreement were formally concluded.
### The institutional structure of SECO
SECO, as the central body for economic policy issues, operates through a complex structure composed of four directorates and the Resources field of performance. Strategic management is entrusted to an executive committee, while the SECO Directorate serves as the central discussion body. With over 900 employees distributed across three locations in Switzerland and 50 detached in 32 countries, the entity manages economic relations and trade policies that influence national market stability. Transparency towards users is ensured by a thematically structured website, which allows quick access to all essential information for economic operators and citizens. The entity's activities range from managing international exchanges to promoting apprenticeships and university internships, thus actively contributing to the Swiss educational and professional system. The introduction of variable tariffs up to 12.5% by the United States raises significant issues for Swiss companies exporting products overseas. The SECO, as the competent authority, is the point of reference for companies needing clarification on the concrete application of these measures based on the Trade Act of 1974.
